#5587. 5 simple ways to feel more positive every day

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Build a brighter outlook with practical habits that can lift your mood, boost your energy, and help you find more joy in everyday life

A positive attitude doesn’t mean pretending everything is perfect or forcing yourself to be happy all the time. Life will always bring stress, disappointments and days when getting out of bed feels like enough of an accomplishment. But the way you respond to those moments can make a difference in how you feel.

The good news is that optimism isn’t something you either have or don’t have. It’s a mindset you can practice, and small everyday habits can help you build it. Sometimes that means changing the way you talk to yourself. Other times, it’s as simple as putting on a favorite song, stepping outside or spending time with someone who makes you feel good.

A positive outlook may also offer benefits beyond a sunnier mood. Research has linked optimism with better overall health, including a lower risk of heart disease and early death. It’s also associated with greater well-being and fewer symptoms of depression. That doesn’t mean positive thinking can solve every problem, but it can help you approach life’s challenges with a little more perspective.

Reader’s Digest shared practical ways to cultivate a more positive attitude, from moving your body and getting enough rest, to volunteering and taking a break from social media. You don’t have to tackle all of them at once. Start with the habits that feel most natural, and give yourself room to make them part of your routine. A more positive day doesn’t have to start with a big transformation. Sometimes it begins with one small choice.

Here are five ways to improve how you feel every day.

It’s easy to become your own toughest critic. You might blame yourself when something goes wrong, assume the worst or turn one mistake into a sweeping judgment about who you are. That kind of internal commentary can chip away at your confidence and make it harder to maintain a positive outlook.

The first step is noticing when it happens. If you catch yourself personalizing a situation, catastrophizing or replaying everything you think you did wrong, pause and question whether those thoughts are helping you. A difficult moment doesn’t have to become a verdict on your entire day, and a mistake doesn’t define your worth.

You don’t need to replace every negative thought with an overly cheerful one. Start by being fairer to yourself. Give yourself the same patience and understanding you would offer a friend who was having a hard time. Over time, that more balanced inner voice can help make room for a more positive attitude.

A favorite song can do more than provide a pleasant soundtrack to your day. According to Reader’s Digest, listening to cheerful music with the intention of improving your mood can make a difference. Additionally, the article notes that you can be a little deliberate about what you play.

Instead of leaving a random playlist running in the background, choose songs that make you feel energized, relaxed or hopeful. It could be an upbeat pop track, an old favorite that brings back good memories or a song that makes you want to sing along.

Music can also be an easy mood reset during an otherwise ordinary day. Put on your headphones during a work break, play something cheerful while making dinner or create a playlist for your morning routine. You don't need a special occasion to enjoy it.

Doing something kind for someone else can give your day a greater sense of purpose, according to Reader’s Digest. Volunteering may help reduce loneliness and create a stronger connection to your community, both of which can contribute to a more positive outlook.

But the reason you volunteer matters, too. Rather than treating it as another obligation to check off your list, look for a cause that genuinely resonates with you. Think about the people or organizations you care about and the kind of help you wish you could have offered someone earlier in your life.

You don't have to commit to a major ongoing role to get started. A few hours at a local organization, helping with a community event or offering practical support to a neighbor can be meaningful ways to give back. The goal is to find a form of service that feels personal rather than performative.

When helping others becomes a genuine expression of what matters to you, it can offer more than a temporary distraction. It can remind you that you have something valuable to contribute.

Stopping to notice something pleasant may sound almost too simple to affect your outlook, but even a small sensory experience can help shift your mood. According to the report, floral scents boosted cheerfulness by improving energy levels and suppressing feelings of depression.

You don't need an elaborate garden or a special occasion to try it. Pause to enjoy flowers on a walk, bring a bouquet into your home or take a moment to appreciate the scent of something blooming nearby. The point is to slow down long enough to notice what's around you.

Being present in the moment can also support a sense of inner peace, according to Reader’s Digest. Instead of rushing through your day while thinking about the next task, give yourself a few seconds to focus on one small thing you enjoy.

You can make the habit more meaningful by keeping track of these moments. A gratitude journal offers a place to record the little things that bring you pleasure, whether that's a pleasant scent, a sunny afternoon or an unexpected kindness. Over time, looking back at those entries can help you recognize how many good moments are tucked into an ordinary week.

When you're exhausted, it's tough to feel optimistic. Fatigue can make everyday frustrations seem bigger and leave you with less patience for the challenges that come your way. A short nap can offer a chance to rest and reset.

There may be emotional benefits, too. According to Reader’s Digest, daytime napping can boost happiness and improve work performance. If you work from home or have some flexibility in your schedule, a little downtime may help you return to the rest of your day feeling more refreshed.

Of course, a nap isn't always practical. If you can't fit one in, try giving yourself a quiet break instead of pushing through exhaustion without stopping. The bigger point is to treat rest as something you need, not a reward you have to earn. Taking care of your energy can make it easier to approach the day with a better attitude.

#5585. Cloudflare shares surge as revenue growth accelerates to 39% and outlook rises

Shares of Cloudflare Inc. jumped more than 14% in late trading today after the connectivity cloud company smashed third-quarter expectations and lifted its full-year outlook well above what Wall Street had been modeling.

The gain more than wiped out an 8% fall in the stock during the regular session.

For the quarter ended on Sept. 30, Cloudflare reported adjusted earnings per share of 38 cents, up from 27 cents in the same quarter of 2025, on revenue of $782.5 million, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 34 cents per share on revenue of $736.8 million.

Revenue growth hit its fastest pace in nearly four years as the annualized run rate crossed $3 billion. Current remaining performance obligations rose 37% from a year earlier. The adjusted operating margin also improved, to 17.5% from 15.3%, after shrinking year-over-year in each of the two prior quarters.

Because stock-based compensation ran to $174.1 million, Cloudflare still lost $34.1 million on an unadjusted basis, compared with a $1.3 million loss a year earlier. Another $11 million went to restructuring from the roughly 1,100 job cuts announced in May. Free cash flow slipped to 10% of revenue from 13% a year ago.

On the product side, short-lived blocking rules that write themselves during a live attack are the core of Adaptive Intelligence, which Cloudflare added to its Bot Management product in late August. AI agents got tools of their own earlier in the month through Cloudflare Wallets and cloudflare.pay, which give an agent an identity handle and will let it pay for services from a stablecoin balance. Federal agencies can now put more sensitive workloads on Cloudflare for Government, which reached FedRAMP High status in August.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Matthew Prince called the period “Cloudflare’s best quarter ever” in the earnings release. Cloudflare has built the development platform for the AI-powered internet, and organizations of every size keep turning to it for protection as digital threats escalate, he said. Prince added that the business has “found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth.”

Cloudflare also named Christian Smith president of revenue today, with responsibility for worldwide sales and revenue operations. He replaces Mark Anderson, who had already said he would retire from the full-time role at year-end. Smith previously ran sales at Splunk Inc. as chief revenue officer.

For the fourth quarter, Cloudflare expects adjusted earnings of 43 cents per share on revenue of $845 million to $846 million. Analysts had forecast 38 cents per share on revenue of $798.2 million.

Cloudflare now expects 2026 revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion, about $97 million above the midpoint of the range it gave in August. Analysts had been looking for $2.87 billion in revenue and $1.26 in adjusted earnings per share for the year, and the company is now guiding to $1.35.

#5584. 4 ways to handle your 401(k) after losing a job

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What to do with your 401(k) after a layoff comes down to four options — leave it, roll it into a new plan or an IRA, or cash out

A layoff ends a paycheck. It does not end ownership of the money already sitting in a 401(k). Every dollar an employee contributed through payroll, along with the investment earnings on those dollars, belongs to that employee regardless of how or why the job ended.

What can shrink is the employer's share. Matching contributions may follow a vesting schedule, which ties ownership of company money to length of service. Any portion that has not vested by the last day of work is generally forfeited. Before choosing a next step, check the plan's vesting records or the most recent account statement to see how much of the balance is fully yours.

Once the vested amount is clear, the decision about what to do with your 401(k) after a layoff becomes a question of where the money should live next. Leaving a job makes it possible to move the account. There are four main paths. The balance can stay in the former employer's plan. It can be rolled into a plan at a future employer. It can be rolled into an individual retirement account, or IRA. Or it can be withdrawn as cash.

These four options are a selection of common choices, not a ranking. Each one fits a different set of circumstances, and the right fit depends on age, cash needs, job prospects and tax situation.

One term comes up repeatedly in any 401(k) rollover after losing a job: the direct rollover. In a direct rollover, the old plan sends the money straight to the receiving account. It never passes through the account holder's hands. This is also called a trustee-to-trustee transfer. Because the money is never paid out to the individual, a direct rollover triggers no income tax and no withholding. The alternative, in which a check goes to the account holder first, carries rules and risks that a direct transfer avoids.

The timing of a layoff can add pressure. Severance may be short, unemployment benefits may not cover every bill, and a large retirement balance can look like a ready source of cash.

The slides that follow take the four options one at a time. Each covers how that path is taxed, which rules govern access to the money and what trade-offs to weigh before filling out any paperwork.

Many 401(k) plans let a laid-off worker keep the balance where it is. The money stays invested in the plan and remains tax-deferred until it is withdrawn.

For balances above $7,000, staying in the plan is the default. Nothing moves unless the former employee asks for a transfer or a withdrawal.

Smaller accounts follow different rules. Under the SECURE 2.0 Act, plans may force out balances of $7,000 or less for distributions made after Dec. 31, 2023. The earlier cutoff was $5,000. A balance of $1,000 or less may be paid out in cash. A balance above $1,000 and up to $7,000 may be moved automatically into an IRA. Anyone with a balance near those thresholds should read the plan's notices closely after leaving.

Staying in the plan comes with limits. A former employee can no longer contribute to the account. Investment choices are confined to the funds on the plan's menu, and the account holder cannot add outside options.

That menu can cut both ways. Some plans offer institutional-class funds or stable-value options that an individual investor may not be able to buy elsewhere. Comparing the plan's lineup and costs with those of other accounts shows whether moving the money gains or loses anything.

The account also keeps its legal shield. The Employee Retirement Income Security Act, or ERISA, gives 401(k) assets strong protection from creditors. That protection continues while the money sits in a former employer's plan.

The Rule of 55 can make staying in the plan worth more to older workers. A worker who leaves a job in or after the calendar year they turn 55 can take withdrawals from that employer's 401(k). Those withdrawals avoid the 10% additional tax on early distributions.

Ordinary income tax still applies to the money withdrawn. For certain public safety workers, the qualifying age is 50 rather than 55.

The rule covers only the plan of the employer the worker just left. It does not apply to IRAs. Rolling the balance into an IRA would give up that penalty-free access. That trade-off matters for anyone in their mid-50s who may need the money before age 59½.

Required minimum distributions also apply to money left in an old 401(k). The starting age depends on birth year under current law, so account holders should confirm their own date with the plan.

Once you start a new job, a direct rollover of your old 401(k) into the new employer's plan keeps the money tax-deferred and puts your retirement savings in one account. This path opens up only after you have been hired and the new plan is ready to take the money.

That timing matters for anyone who has just been laid off. A person who is still looking for work has no new plan to roll into. Until a job and a plan are in place, the balance has to sit somewhere else, such as the former employer's plan.

The new plan also has to accept rollovers. Not every 401(k) plan does. Some plans also set a waiting period before a new hire can participate in the plan. The plan administrator or the plan's summary documents can confirm both points.

Requesting a direct rollover keeps the move free of income tax and withholding.

Each type of money keeps its tax treatment. Pre-tax contributions and their earnings go into the pre-tax side of the new plan. Roth 401(k) money goes into a Roth account, but only if the new plan offers one. A worker with Roth savings should check for that feature before starting the transfer.

Money held in an employer 401(k) plan has strong protection from creditors under ERISA, the federal law that governs these plans. Rolling into a new employer's 401(k) keeps that protection in place.

Loan access is a separate question. If the new plan permits loans, consolidating the balance there can preserve the ability to borrow against retirement savings. Not every plan offers loans. Whether borrowing remains possible depends on the new plan's rules.

The investment lineup changes, too. Once the money moves, the new plan's fund menu and fees apply to it. Comparing the new plan's menu and costs with the old plan's shows what the switch would change before any money moves.

A direct rollover of pre-tax 401(k) money into a traditional IRA is not a taxable event. It also usually gives the account holder a far wider choice of investments than an employer plan's menu offers.

This path does not depend on landing a new job. The account holder chooses the IRA provider, not an employer. Fees and services vary widely from one provider to the next. The account holder can compare those differences before the money moves.

The route the money takes shapes the tax result. A direct rollover moves the balance with nothing withheld. If the plan pays the money to the account holder instead, it must withhold 20% for federal income tax.

That indirect route starts a 60-day clock. To avoid tax on the full balance, the account holder must deposit the entire original amount into the IRA within that window. The deposit has to include the 20% the plan withheld, which means covering that portion from other funds. Any shortfall not deposited in time is taxed. A direct rollover avoids both the withholding and the deadline.

The type of IRA also shapes the outcome. Pre-tax 401(k) money moved into a traditional IRA stays tax-deferred. Pre-tax money moved into a Roth IRA counts as a conversion. The converted amount is added to ordinary income for that year and taxed as such. Money already held in a Roth 401(k) can move into a Roth IRA without tax on the rollover itself.

Creditor protection also changes once the money leaves an employer plan. ERISA, the federal law governing employer plans, gives 401(k) assets strong protection from creditors. IRAs carry federal protection in bankruptcy, but that protection is capped. Outside bankruptcy, the shield around an IRA depends on the law of the account holder's state.

Early access works differently, too. Withdrawals from an IRA before age 59½ generally face a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies. A worker who could have used the Rule of 55 to draw from a former employer's 401(k) loses that option once the money sits in an IRA.

Cashing out a 401(k) turns the balance into ordinary income for the year the money arrives. Before age 59½, the withdrawal generally also carries a 10% additional tax unless an exception, such as the Rule of 55, applies.

The 10% charge sits on top of regular income tax, not in place of it. It is often called an early-withdrawal penalty, though the tax code treats it as an additional tax. Even when an exception removes the 10% charge, ordinary income tax is still owed on the withdrawal.

The check a person receives will be smaller than the account balance. The plan must withhold 20% of a cash distribution for federal income tax. That withholding is a prepayment, not a final figure.

The actual tax owed depends on the person's total income and tax bracket for the year. It may be higher or lower than the amount withheld. If it is higher, the difference comes due at filing time. If it is lower, the excess comes back as part of a refund. The 10% additional tax, when it applies, is settled on the tax return as well. State income tax may also apply, depending on where the person lives.

The timing of a layoff affects the math. A year cut short by a job loss may bring lower wages than usual. A large withdrawal still adds to that year's income. It can push part of that income into a higher bracket.

A cash withdrawal also ends tax deferral on whatever amount comes out. Money left in a plan or rolled over keeps growing without current tax. Cashed-out money does not. Federal rules allow 60 days after a distribution to roll it into an IRA or another plan. Once that window closes, the money can no longer be rolled back into a tax-deferred account.

Plan loans add another layer. An outstanding 401(k) loan usually comes due or is offset after separation from service. An offset means the unpaid loan balance is subtracted from the account and treated as a distribution. That amount is taxable like any other cash withdrawal. Rules in place since the 2017 tax law give extra time when the offset happens because of leaving the job. In that case, the person has until the tax-filing deadline for that year, including extensions. Within that window, the offset amount can be rolled into an IRA or another plan to avoid tax on it.

#5582. How Can Humanity Become Friends with the Ocean?

BEIJING, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A news report from China.org.cn on China's efforts in marine ecological governance:

"Look, white dolphins!" Such excited cries can often be heard along the coast of Xiamen, a city in east China's Fujian Province.

The Indo-Pacific humpback dolphin, commonly known as the Chinese white dolphin, is considered Class I nationally protected wildlife in China. As apex predators in coastal waters, these dolphins are regarded as a barometer of marine ecosystem health. Back in the 1990s, however, rising shipping activity, coastal reclamation and nearâshore development severely encroached on their habitats.

To minimize disturbances to dolphin habitats, Xiamen established China's first provincialâlevel nature reserve dedicated to Chinese white dolphins in 1997. Since then, the city has continuously refined its coastal governance approaches, restricted activities with significant environmental impacts, and promoted crossâregional collaboration in conservation. Many other oceanâfriendly initiatives have also been rolled out. These include restoring mangrove wetland ecosystems; implementing an "offshore sanitation" mechanism and organizing public beachâcleanâup campaigns to regularly remove floating marine debris; and releasing nearly 8 billion aquatic animals across 18 species through stock enhancement programs. As a result, populations of several fish species, such as the wild large yellow croaker and yellowfin seabream, have returned to Xiamen Bay.

Recently, "AI bodyguards" have joined the conservation effort. Highâdefinition cameras, drones and intelligent recognition systems track dolphin activity roundâtheâclock. Automatic alerts are issued whenever vessels approach the dolphins in violation of regulations. Researchers have also created individual digital profiles for each dolphin, identifying them by their dorsalâfin shapes and body spot patterns, while recording their movement trajectories.

Xiamen is a microcosm of China's efforts in marine ecological governance â forging ahead boldly yet never walking alone.

Over the decades, China has taken a series of concrete steps: from founding its first marine nature reserve in 1963, to proposing the goal of "building a strong maritime nation," and publishing the white paper "Marine EcoâEnvironmental Protection in China"; from drawing marine ecological protection red lines, to actively engaging with the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development and signing major international agreements on marine conservation, including the UN Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (UN BBNJ).

For decades, China has been answering a vital question through concrete action: how can humanity coexist harmoniously with the ocean and create mutual benefits?

The answer is becoming increasingly clearer. Today, China's extensive coastline features clean waters and pristine beaches, with fish swimming freely and seabirds soaring overhead. Not long ago, China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was named a UN World Restoration Flagship. Now, the 21st Xiamen World Ocean Week is officially inaugurated, bringing together experts, scholars and representatives from various countries and international organizations to discuss marine conservation and harmonious coexistence between humanity and the ocean. In marine ecological protection and governance, China is not only a proactive participant and practitioner, but also a contributor to sharing experience and shaping future approaches.

Along Xiamen's shoreline, the sea breeze blows gently as children run after the waves, echoing the ongoing story of humanity and the ocean.

#5581. OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations

OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built.

It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies.

The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects.

OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays.

It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC.

Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”

OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions.

The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions.

OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress.

Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. Anthropic PBC made a similar commitment in February.

#5580. What's negotiable in a severance package: 10 terms to raise before you sign

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What's negotiable in a severance package goes beyond the check, from COBRA premiums and equity vesting to release terms, references and payment timing

Private employers in the U.S. have no federal obligation to pay severance. That fact shapes any conversation about leaving a job with a package. When an employment contract, a written company policy or a union agreement sets the terms, the employer may be bound by them. When none of those applies, the package is an offer, and an offer can be answered with a counteroffer.

Employers usually attach a condition to that offer. Severance is typically paid in exchange for signing a release of legal claims against the company. That release is the main thing the employer receives in the deal. The employee is giving up something of value. As a result, the rest of the separation agreement becomes part of the exchange, not just the size of the check.

That is why the question of what's negotiable in a severance package reaches well beyond pay. A separation agreement can address how long health coverage is subsidized and what happens to unvested stock. It can settle whether a partial-year bonus is paid and how much time a worker gets to review the document. It can also set the wording of the release and the reach of any non-compete or confidentiality clause. Other terms can cover the reference a former manager gives and the way the money arrives.

Some of these terms rest on federal law. These include the WARN Act's notice rules and COBRA health continuation. They also include the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act's minimum review periods for workers aged 40 or older. Others depend on plan documents, award agreements or state law. Many are purely contractual, meaning they exist only if both sides agree to write them down.

The 10 items below are a selection of terms that commonly come up in severance package negotiation. They are not a complete list, and not every employer will agree to every request. Each slide explains what the term covers, what rules shape it and what an employee can ask for.

This guide is limited to the U.S. Severance rules and notice requirements differ from country to country. It is general information, not legal advice. An employment lawyer can review a specific agreement against the contract, policies and state law that apply to it.

No federal law requires private employers in the U.S. to pay severance. When no employment contract, company policy or union agreement fixes the amount, the figure in an employer's offer is a starting point that can be negotiated.

Severance pay is usually set in one of four ways. An individual employment contract may spell it out. A written company policy or severance plan may lay out who qualifies and how much they receive. A collective bargaining agreement may cover it for union members. Or the employer may simply make an offer at the time of separation.

Each source affects how much room there is to bargain over money. A contract or union agreement that names a figure creates an obligation the employer has already committed to in writing. A written policy can work the same way. It can also cap the amount the employer is prepared to pay. An offer made with no document behind it leaves the most room to move.

One practical step is to find out which source applies. That means rereading an offer letter or employment agreement for any clause on termination or separation pay. It also means checking the employee handbook, benefits materials or any separate severance plan document the company has distributed. Union members can look to the terms of their collective bargaining agreement.

If a written policy exists, compare the offer with it. An employee can ask directly whether the proposed amount matches the policy, exceeds it or falls short of it. A shortfall is a concrete point to raise. A match signals that the dollar figure may be harder to move. That can shift attention to other terms in the package.

Where none of those documents applies, the number in the offer reflects the employer's own business decision. An employee in that position can reply in writing with a different figure. The employee can also ask the employer to explain how it arrived at the proposed amount.

The federal WARN Act generally requires employers with 100 or more employees to give 60 calendar days' notice before a plant closing or mass layoff. Pay and benefits covering that period can stand in for the advance warning itself.

That substitution affects what a severance offer contains. Pay in lieu of notice under WARN is tied to a legal requirement. It is not the same thing as a voluntary severance payment, even when an employer provides both at the same time.

An employee can ask the employer to state in writing which part of the package covers the notice period and which part is severance. When the two are blended into one figure, it is harder to see how much of the offer goes beyond what the law already required.

WARN does not reach every exit. An employer with fewer than 100 employees falls outside the federal rule. So does a single termination that is not part of a plant closing or mass layoff. For those departures, notice is a matter of contract.

An employment agreement, an offer letter or a written company policy may already set a notice period. Where none of them does, the two sides can settle the length of notice in the separation agreement. An employee whose contract specifies notice can also check whether the offer honors it.

Garden leave is one way to structure a contractual notice period. The employee stays on the payroll through the notice period but is not expected to do any work. The details come from the agreement, not from federal law.

Several garden-leave terms are open to discussion. They include how long the period runs and whether benefits continue during it. Another is whether the employee may start a new job before it ends.

Pay in lieu of notice outside WARN follows the same contractual logic. The employer pays for the notice period instead of having the employee work through it. The job then ends sooner than it otherwise would.

An employee who is unsure whether WARN applies can ask how many workers the action affects. Another useful question is whether the employer treats it as a covered plant closing or mass layoff.

COBRA generally lets covered employees keep their group health coverage for up to 18 months after a job loss. An employer can agree in a severance package to pay part or all of the premium for a set period.

COBRA protects access to coverage, not its price. The former employee typically pays the full premium plus up to 2 percent for administration. That brings the total to as much as 102 percent of the premium.

The full premium includes any portion the employer covered while the person was on the payroll. As a result, the monthly bill after a layoff can be much higher than the health deduction that used to appear on a pay stub.

That gap is why a premium subsidy is a common request in a separation agreement. Under a subsidy, the employer pays some or all of the COBRA cost for a defined number of months. The worker keeps the same group coverage. What changes is who pays for it.

A subsidy's terms are open to negotiation like the rest of the package. A departing employee can ask for a longer subsidy period, a larger share of the premium or both. If more than one person is enrolled under the worker's plan, the request should spell out whose coverage the subsidy applies to.

Precise wording matters. A clear agreement states the start and end dates of the subsidy. It also states the dollar amount or percentage the employer will cover. It should say what happens if the former employee gains coverage through a new job before the subsidy period ends. Vague terms on those points can lead to disputes later.

Plan details also shape what a worker can expect. Coverage length and cost can vary with the plan and with the size of the employer. The 18-month period and the 102 percent ceiling are general rules, not guarantees for every worker. Checking the plan's own terms with the employer's benefits staff before signing shows what a subsidy would actually be worth.

A premium subsidy is a separate term from the cash payment. It can be requested even when the employer will not move on the severance pay figure itself.

Unvested stock options, restricted stock units and similar awards are governed by the equity plan and the individual award agreement, not by the severance offer alone. A separation agreement can change those default terms by accelerating vesting or by giving a departing employee more time to exercise options.

Vesting is the schedule that turns a grant into something the employee actually owns. An award that has not vested by the last day of work is handled however the plan documents say it should be. That makes those documents the starting point for any request. The plan sets the default rules. The award agreement sets the terms of each specific grant, including its vesting schedule and what happens when employment ends.

Acceleration is a request to vest some or all of the unvested portion as part of the exit. The ask can cover a full grant, a fixed number of shares or options, or the tranche that would have vested next. Whether an employer agrees depends on its own plan and on its willingness to depart from the standard terms in this particular agreement.

The exercise window matters only for stock options. An option is the right to buy shares at a set price, and the holder pays that price to exercise it. A restricted stock unit, by contrast, delivers shares or their value once it vests and does not require an exercise payment. Options left unexercised when the post-employment period closes are handled under the plan's terms. A separation agreement can extend that period beyond what the plan provides.

Incentive stock options (ISOs) carry a tax condition. They generally lose their favorable tax treatment if exercised more than three months after employment ends. A longer window still gives an ISO holder more time to decide whether to buy. Any exercise after that point, though, generally gives up the ISO tax advantage. A tax adviser can weigh that trade-off before the agreement is signed.

Non-qualified stock options do not have a single standard post-termination exercise period. Plans differ, and the award agreement is the place to find the actual deadline. An extension negotiated in a separation agreement can state the new deadline in writing. It can also specify which grants the extension covers.

Money already in motion at the time of a layoff — a bonus, a commission or unused vacation — can often be negotiated. Whether accrued vacation must be paid out depends on state law and company policy. Bonus and commission payouts depend on plan terms and contract language.

Accrued paid time off can carry a legal floor. Some states treat earned vacation as wages. Where that rule applies, a vacation balance is a pay question rather than a perk to bargain over. In other places, the company's written policy usually settles the matter. That makes the employee handbook and any PTO policy the first documents to read before a severance conversation.

Where neither state law nor company policy requires a payout, the unused balance becomes something to ask for. It can be raised alongside the severance figure itself rather than handled as a separate dispute.

Bonuses work differently. The answer usually sits in a bonus plan document, an offer letter or an employment contract. The exact wording matters. A plan might tie payment to company results, individual targets, a specific payout date or some mix of those conditions. Reading those terms closely shows whether a partial-year bonus is owed, partly owed or left to the employer's discretion.

Even when the plan does not require a payout, an employee can request one. The request can take two forms. A pro-rated bonus pays a share that reflects the portion of the year already worked. A full bonus pays the entire target amount, as if the employee had stayed through the bonus period. Either version can be written into the separation agreement.

Commissions follow similar logic. A salesperson may have deals that closed, or were close to closing, near the last day of work. The commission plan and any contract language determine whether those deals generate pay after departure. If the terms are unclear, the separation agreement can spell out which deals count, how much each one pays and when the money arrives.

Workers aged 40 or older must get at least 21 days to consider a severance agreement that releases age-discrimination claims. The minimum rises to 45 days when the offer is part of a group exit program. Signers then have seven days to revoke.

Those deadlines come from the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act. This federal law sets conditions on how employers can ask older employees to give up age-discrimination claims. The review period is a floor, not a ceiling. An employer can offer longer, and an employee who needs more time can ask for it.

The two lengths depend on how the separation is structured. An individual departure that is not part of a group program falls under the 21-day minimum. The 45-day minimum applies when the release is offered to a group of employees through an exit program.

Group programs carry an added requirement. The employer must disclose the job titles and ages of the employees selected for the program. It must also disclose the job titles and ages of those who were not selected. That information lets an older worker see how age lined up with the selection decisions before deciding whether to sign.

The seven-day revocation window runs after the signature, not before it. It gives the employee a chance to back out of the release after committing to it in writing. The review period and the revocation period are separate, and one does not replace the other.

Workers under 40 get no federal minimum review period. Any deadline in their offer is set by the employer. That makes the deadline a term like any other in the agreement. An employee can ask for an extension, especially when the document is long or touches equity, benefits and restrictive covenants.

A severance agreement often bundles many separate terms into one document. Time to read it closely, compare it against company policy and plan documents and raise questions comes before negotiating any of those terms.

Severance is typically paid only after the departing employee signs a release of legal claims against the employer. The wording of that release can be negotiated. It can be narrowed in scope, or made mutual so the employer also gives up claims.

A release is the clause in a separation agreement that gives the employer legal protection. In exchange for the severance payment, the employee agrees not to pursue claims tied to the job or the way it ended.

Release language is often drafted broadly. A standard version may cover every claim the employee has or could have, known or unknown, against the company. It may also extend to a long list of related parties. An employee can ask for edits that tighten that scope. One request is to limit the release to claims arising before the date of signing. Another is to spell out exceptions, such as the right to enforce the severance agreement itself.

A mutual release changes the balance of the document. Under a one-sided release, only the employee gives something up. Under a mutual version, the employer also agrees not to bring claims against the former employee. Some employees ask for this to reduce the risk of a later dispute over their conduct on the job. The employer may decline, and the request is a matter of bargaining rather than a right.

Some rights cannot be signed away, whatever the release says. These include claims for vested benefits, workers' compensation and unemployment benefits. A release also cannot remove an employee's right to file a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. What an employee can give up is the right to collect money personally from such a charge.

The effect of a release depends on the facts of each case and the law that applies. Nothing here is legal advice. An employment lawyer can read the exact language before the agreement is signed.

Separation agreements often include restrictions on where a departing employee can work, who they can contact and what they can say or share. The duration, geography and scope of each restriction can be negotiated before the agreement is signed.

A non-compete limits where a former employee can work next. It usually sets a period of time, a geographic area and a definition of competing work. Each of those three elements is its own point of negotiation. A shorter period, a smaller territory or a narrower description of the competing business can each reduce how much the clause limits a job search.

Whether a non-compete can be enforced depends on state law. Those rules differ from one state to another. The same clause can carry different weight depending on where the employee works. An agreement may also include a choice-of-law clause naming the state whose law governs the contract.

The Federal Trade Commission issued a rule in 2024 aimed at non-compete agreements. A federal court blocked it. The rule never took effect.

A non-solicit clause works differently. It restricts a former employee from reaching out to clients, customers or co-workers to win their business or recruit them. An employee can ask to limit it to clients they personally handled. They can also ask for a shorter time frame. Another request is an exception for contacts who approach the former employee on their own.

Confidentiality terms cover an employer's nonpublic information. Some also cover the terms of the severance agreement itself. An employee can ask for a precise definition of what counts as confidential. They can also ask for written exceptions, such as conversations with a spouse, an attorney or a tax adviser.

Non-disparagement clauses bar negative statements about the employer. As drafted, these clauses often bind only the employee. One counter is to make the clause mutual. The employer would then agree not to disparage the departing worker. Some employees also ask the company to direct specific managers or executives to follow it.

Restrictive covenants in a separation agreement can stay in force after the severance payments end. Their wording shapes what a former employee can do in a next job, with past clients and in public comments.

An employee leaving under a severance agreement can ask for an agreed reference statement, an agreed internal and external announcement, and neutral wording of the departure. None of these is a legal entitlement. Each is a contractual ask that an employer can accept, modify or decline.

An agreed reference statement is a set text the employer commits to using when a prospective employer calls or writes about the departing worker. Its value lies in predictability. Both sides know in advance what will be said. The wording can also be reviewed before the agreement is signed.

A worker can ask who at the company will handle reference requests. Routing those inquiries to a named person or department sends them to someone bound by the agreed language. Without that step, a request may reach a former colleague who does not know the terms exist.

The announcement works the same way. An internal message tells colleagues that someone has left. An external one reaches clients, vendors or industry contacts. A departing employee can ask to see and approve the text of both before they go out, and can ask that they be issued at an agreed time.

Neutral wording covers how the exit itself is described. Phrases such as "terminated," "laid off" and "left the company" read differently to an outsider. A worker can ask that the agreement and any related documents use language that does not suggest fault.

Some employers will go further and agree to describe the exit as a resignation. That label can shape how the departure is characterized to future employers and former colleagues. It does not control the outcome of an unemployment claim, however. A state unemployment agency makes its own decision about eligibility. The wording in a separation agreement does not settle that question.

A worker who expects to file for unemployment benefits can weigh how a resignation label fits with that claim before agreeing to it.

These terms are only as dependable as the document that contains them. A spoken assurance about references or announcements is harder to point to later than language written into the signed agreement. Asking for the exact text, rather than a general promise, gives both sides the same words to rely on.

Severance can be paid as a single lump sum or spread out in installments, and an employee can negotiate that structure. The choice affects when the money arrives and how much federal tax is withheld from it.

A lump sum delivers the full amount in one payment. Installments divide the same total into a series of payments over a set period. These payments can follow the employer's regular payroll cycle. A series of payments spreads the income across a longer stretch. If the schedule runs long enough, it can extend into a new calendar year.

Federal income tax withholding on severance follows the rules for supplemental wages. An employer can withhold at a flat 22 percent rate on supplemental wages up to $1 million. Amounts above that threshold are withheld at 37 percent. Withholding is a prepayment toward tax, not the final bill. The amount actually owed is settled when the employee files a return. The flat rate can therefore end up higher or lower than a person's real tax liability.

Payment timing has limits of its own. Section 409A of the Internal Revenue Code sets rules for deferred compensation. Those timing rules can affect how a severance payment schedule is written. Anyone asking for a different schedule can have a tax adviser review how the change fits within those rules.

Severance can also interact with unemployment insurance. Whether severance pay reduces unemployment benefits depends on the state. The state unemployment agency is the place to check how a particular payment structure will be treated.

The agreement can also cover more than the payment itself. An employee can ask for outplacement services, which provide job-search support after the exit. A request for legal-fee reimbursement can cover the cost of having a lawyer review the agreement. Some employees ask to move the termination date later so it falls after an upcoming equity vesting date. None of these extras is guaranteed. Each is a request the employer can accept or decline.

#5578. 10 world leaders ranked by salary, from Australia's PM to Spain's head of government

Free daily briefing on global business news.

See how 10 world leaders' salaries compare in U.S. dollars and against the minimum wage paid to workers in their own countries.

Every national leader cashes a paycheck that the public funds, and the sum draws scrutiny from the people footing the bill. Citizens who argue about wages, taxes, and the cost of living want to know whether the person in charge shares their economic reality or occupies a different one. The question carries weight beyond curiosity. A leader's compensation can signal how a country values public office. It also offers a rough gauge of the distance between those who govern and those who earn the legal wage floor. Lining up those paychecks across borders creates a puzzle of its own. Each country sets the amount in a separate currency and under separate laws.

Converting every salary into U.S. dollars yields a neat table, yet the result says more about exchange rates and the size of each economy than about the job itself. A different yardstick cuts closer to the issue readers raise. Dividing a leader's annual salary by the local full-time minimum wage shows how many of the country's lowest-paid workers it would take to match the person at the top. The measure keeps every comparison inside a single economy, with one currency and one set of prices. It can reshuffle the order a dollar ranking produces, lifting some countries and pulling others down. Salary and wealth differ, too. A generous salary does not equal a large net worth. The numbers that follow track what each office pays. They say nothing about what any officeholder owns.

Neto gathered pay figures for 10 leaders, limiting the list to those whose 2026 earnings it could confirm through an official source. Germany's chancellor fell outside the list for lack of such a confirmed amount. The publication orders the 10 by approximate U.S. dollar value and expresses each total as a multiple of the local full-time minimum wage. Several entries depart from the 2026 baseline. France's total comes from a presidential payslip dated January 2024, which the publication expects has not changed. Spain's reflects the sum disbursed in 2025. Mexico's total folds in the year-end bonus and benefits. The bundled total and the base salaries elsewhere measure different things. Italy's entry rests on parliamentary pay.

Australia's prime minister commands A$622,102 a year, about US$433,900 and the largest dollar sum of any leader on this list. The figure begins with the A$239,270 salary every federal parliamentarian receives. The office layers on another 160%, or A$382,832, which turns a lawmaker's standard pay into the richest package in the group.

The premium by itself outstrips the parliamentary salary by A$143,562, a margin equal to 60% of that salary. Holding the office supplies 61.5% of the total, and the seat in parliament provides the other 38.5%. Put another way, the top job pays 2.6 times what an ordinary member earns. The loading alone comes to roughly US$267,000, more than the entire annual pay of Britain's prime minister or any leader below that entry. The standard parliamentary salary, valued near US$166,900, would by itself exceed the full packages of the leaders of Mexico, Italy, Brazil, and Spain.

Australia's Remuneration Tribunal, an independent body, sets the base salary on which the prime minister's pay rests. The tribunal said that federal politicians' pay had to be fair and comparable with other earnings. It added that the level had to draw in and retain capable people. Any shift in the base passes through the 160% loading. Each extra dollar there adds A$2.60 to the prime minister's pay.

The prime minister's pay equals 12 times what a full-time worker on Australia's minimum wage earns, a smaller multiple than the presidents of the U.S., Mexico, and Brazil post despite their lower dollar totals. Working back from the multiple puts the full-time wage floor near A$51,800 a year. The parliamentary salary on its own runs to about 4.6 times that floor. A wage floor of that size keeps the gap between Australia's top office and its lowest-paid full-time workers near the middle of the group, even as the dollar figure exceeds every other leader's.

The U.S. president receives $400,000 a year, 27 times the pay of a full-time worker on the federal minimum wage. The salary appears in federal statute as a fixed dollar amount. Raising it would mean rewriting the law itself.

A $50,000 expense allowance arrives on top of the base pay, lifting the full package to $450,000. Counting the allowance, the total reaches about 30 times a full-time federal minimum-wage income. The salary alone falls about $33,900 short of the Australian prime minister's converted pay, the single entry on the list worth more in dollars. The gap between the two top earners amounts to less than a tenth of the U.S. figure.

Former presidents keep collecting public money after they leave office. Their pension matches a Cabinet secretary's pay, which stands at $253,100 in 2026. Departing the job trims the yearly payment by $146,900 from the presidential salary. The benefit equals about 63% of a sitting president's pay and about 17 times what a full-time federal minimum-wage worker takes in over a year. Even in retirement, a former president outpaces the lowest-paid full-time worker by a wide margin.

The federal minimum wage accounts for much of the 27-times gap. It has stayed at $7.25 an hour since 2009, which works out to about $15,080 a year for full-time work. The floor has gone 17 years without an increase as of 2026. A wage stuck that long will inflate any ratio that uses it as the divisor.

Most states set a higher minimum of their own. A full-time worker in one of those states makes more than $15,080 a year, which pulls that worker's multiple below 27. Neto attributes the extreme U.S. showing on this measure to the federal rate. The 27-times multiple tracks a stalled federal wage floor as much as it tracks the size of the presidential paycheck.

Canada's prime minister earns C$435,400 a year, about US$305,300, under pay rates that took effect April 1, 2026. The sum splits into two equal halves. A seat in the House of Commons brings C$217,700, and leading the government adds an identical C$217,700. In euros, the package is worth about €273,000. Canada prices the premiership at one more legislator's paycheck, no more and no less.

Britain's and Ireland's leaders pair a legislative salary with pay for the top office, though the two pieces differ in size in each country. Canada's matching halves leave no ambiguity about the premium. Taking charge of the government doubles what a member of Parliament earns.

Canada's federal minimum wage climbed to C$18.15 an hour in April 2026, the same month the new parliamentary pay began. A worker earning that wage across a full-time year collects about C$37,750. The prime minister's total equals 11.5 times that income. Measured by the hour over the same full-time year, the leader's pay works out to about C$209, set against the C$18.15 floor.

Each half of the package would amount to nearly six times a full-time minimum wage income on its own. The parliamentary salary by itself clears the floor by a wide margin. The supplement for running the government repeats that distance a second time.

Canada's total sits third among the 10 leaders in dollar terms, behind Australia and the U.S. Canada's leader trails the U.S. president by about US$94,700, yet Canada's multiple comes to less than half the American one. The two leaders stand closer together in currency than in their separation from the lowest-paid worker at home.

Australia's prime minister collects about US$128,600 more than Canada's, but the minimum wage multiples of the two countries differ by half a point. A full-time Canadian minimum wage income equals about 8.7% of the prime minister's annual pay.

Ireland's Taoiseach earns €256,311 a year, about US$286,600, and the total stacks two separate lines of pay. A TD salary of €119,467 forms the base. The office of Taoiseach adds €136,844 on top of the seat in parliament. Both rates took effect June 1, 2026.

The leadership portion outstrips the parliamentary share by €17,377. Running the government accounts for about 53.4% of the package. Canada divides its prime minister's earnings into two identical halves. Ireland tilts the balance toward the office, attaching a sum worth about 115% of the TD rate. The design attaches more money to leading the country than to holding a seat.

The Taoiseach's income equals nine times what a full-time minimum-wage worker in Ireland makes in a year. Five of the nine leaders whose countries set a statutory minimum wage show a wider gap: Australia, Canada, the U.S., Mexico, and Brazil. Ireland's drop from fourth on dollar value to sixth on this yardstick suggests its lowest-paid full-time workers stand closer to their leader than counterparts in those five countries stand to theirs. Canada offers the sharpest contrast. The Canadian prime minister outearns the Taoiseach in dollars and also sits farther from the country's wage floor.

Ireland's leader also outpaces every other European entry on the list in dollar terms. France, the U.K., and Spain each post a smaller multiple of the minimum wage, and Italy sets no statutory floor at all. Among the European entries, Ireland pairs the biggest dollar paycheck with the widest gap between the head of government and the lowest-paid worker.

A few Irish office holders hand back part of their pay. As a result, the €256,311 figure reflects an entitlement, and the sum reaching any given holder may come in lower.

The Taoiseach supplement by itself exceeds the entire sum Spain paid its head of government in 2025.

Britain's prime minister earns £174,039 for 2026-27, about US$230,300, even after turning down part of the pay attached to the top job. The ministerial entitlement stands at £83,837 a year. The prime minister claims £75,440 of it and leaves £8,397 unclaimed. As a result, the office holder accepts about 90% of the available sum.

Claiming the full amount would lift the annual package to £182,436. The unclaimed portion looks small against a six-figure income. Even so, the figures list the entitlement and the claim as two separate numbers, which marks the lower amount as a choice the office holder makes.

A seat in Parliament supplies the larger slice of the money. The £98,599 MP salary accounts for about 57% of the package. In practice, the parliamentary role pays more than the prime ministerial one. The imbalance would persist even with the full entitlement in hand, because £98,599 still exceeds £83,837 by £14,762.

Britain splits the money in the opposite direction from Canada and Australia. Canada pays its prime minister the same amount for leading the government as for serving as an MP. Australia's top-up exceeds the base parliamentary salary. Britain's claimed ministerial pay equals about 77% of the MP salary, and even the full entitlement reaches only about 85%.

The British premier's pay equals about seven times the local full-time minimum wage, a narrow spread by the standards of this list. Neto pairs the U.K. with Spain as the two countries with the smallest gaps, both sitting around six to seven times. France's president, one spot lower in dollar terms, shows a wider multiple than Britain.

The decision to claim less feeds into the narrow spread. A smaller claim shrinks the package, and a smaller package pulls the multiple down. The distance between the office and the lowest-paid full-time worker owes part of its modesty to the prime minister's restraint.

France's president grossed €16,039.71 a month in January 2024, and 12 such payments add up to €192,477 a year. The salary equals about US$215,200, which slots France below Britain and above Mexico among the 10 leaders. The annual total matches 12 identical monthly installments, with none of the extra 13th payment Brazil's president receives.

The president collects 8.6 times the annual earnings of a full-time worker on France's minimum wage. Working backward from that ratio puts the French wage floor near €22,400 a year. Ireland's Taoiseach stands at nine times while drawing about US$71,400 more in dollars. Dividing the Irish total by nine yields a floor close to €28,500. The eurozone neighbor guarantees its lowest earners about €6,100 more each year than France does.

Britain's prime minister earns about US$15,100 more than the French president yet sits at seven times the local minimum wage, a tighter distance from the bottom of the scale. France's smaller salary and wider multiple mean Britain's floor runs higher in dollar terms. The same arithmetic puts the British minimum near US$32,900 a year, against some US$25,000 for France.

France, Ireland, and Britain form a European cluster of single-digit multiples, far from the U.S. at 27 and Brazil at 29. The French gap amounts to less than a third of the American one. France's salary also exceeds Mexico's full presidential package, bonus and benefits included, by about US$58,100. Yet Mexico's president sits at 25 times the local minimum wage, close to triple the French ratio. France pays its president more in dollars than Mexico does, yet the French salary stays far closer to its country's lowest legal wage.

France's civil service pay scales have stayed frozen since July 2023. Any increase in the French minimum wage would pull the 8.6 multiple down as long as the president's monthly gross holds at €16,039.71.

Mexico's president takes home MX$134,290 a month after deductions, and the full yearly package reaches MX$2,882,131, equal to some US$157,100 or €140,500, once the year-end bonus and benefits join base pay. The monthly net figure has held at that level since 2025.

Twelve months of net pay add up to MX$1,611,480, or 56% of the annual total. The remaining 44% stays outside the monthly deposit. A president reading a pay stub sees a little more than half of what the office delivers over a year.

Mexico's total pay equals 25 times the local full-time minimum wage, which puts a full year at that wage near MX$115,000. A single month of the president's net pay outstrips what a minimum-wage worker earns across 12 months.

The Mexican gap comes close to the American one on a dollar amount less than half the size. The U.S. president's US$400,000 salary is more than 2.5 times Mexico's compensation, yet the American multiple of 27 sits two above Mexico's. Canada offers a sharper contrast. Its prime minister earns 1.9 times as much as Mexico's president in dollar terms, while the Canadian multiple of 11.5 comes to less than half of Mexico's.

Mexico's earnings come in below the dollar pay of six other leaders on the list, yet the president's distance from the lowest-paid full-time worker trails only Brazil and the U.S. The total edges past Italy's US$140,000, the next figure down, by US$17,100. Dollar totals, in Mexico's case, understate how far the president stands from the country's minimum-wage earners.

A federal law governing public servants' pay in Mexico bars anyone in public service from earning more than the president. As a result, the president's salary sets a legal ceiling for the whole state payroll. A freeze at the top holds that ceiling in place for every other official on the government payroll.

Giorgia Meloni draws €0 as Italy's prime minister, and all €125,220 of her official annual pay, worth about US$140,000, flows from her seat in parliament. She stands alone among the 10 leaders as the one whose head-of-government post pays nothing.

Meloni has declared that she accepts no salary for running the government. Italian law bars a prime minister from adding the government salary to an MP's wage. The rule keeps the two incomes from merging into one larger package, and she retains only her parliamentary earnings.

Canada's prime minister, Ireland's Taoiseach, and Britain's prime minister each collect a government salary on top of parliamentary pay, the doubling Italian law rules out. Each of them brings home two paychecks for the same dual role Meloni holds. Italy's arrangement leaves her with one.

Her parliamentary salary amounts to €10,435 gross each month, plus allowances. Twelve months at that rate produce €125,220, which shows the annual figure counts base salary alone. The allowances lift her income from public office above that total, by an amount the list leaves undisclosed.

Meloni's legislative wage by itself outstrips the full packages of two other leaders on the list, Brazil's president and Spain's head of government. Italy and Spain both pay in euros, which strips exchange rates out of the second comparison. Her MP salary runs €29,276 above what the Spanish leader received in 2025.

Italy has no statutory minimum wage, which leaves Meloni as the only leader on the list without a pay multiple. The other nine entries each show how many times their leader out-earns a full-time worker on the legal floor. Italy supplies no such benchmark, and the distance between her pay and the bottom of its labor market goes unmeasured.

Italian taxpayers fund Meloni at a lawmaker's rate, and the premiership adds nothing to the bill. Her eighth-place spot in the dollar ordering reflects a legislative wage.

Brazil's president takes in R$602,760 a year, about US$120,700, a sum 29 times the country's minimum wage and the widest gap among the 10 leaders. A worker on that minimum would need about 29 years of full-time labor to earn what the president collects in one.

The money arrives in 13 installments of R$46,366.19, one more payment than the calendar has months. A single installment equals about 28.6 times the R$1,621 minimum wage set for 2026. The gap stays about as wide paycheck by paycheck as it does across the full year.

Brazil's dollar total sits ninth of 10, ahead of only Spain's head of government at US$107,300. A margin of US$13,400 separates the two sums, yet Spain's leader receives 5.6 times the local minimum wage, a ratio less than one-fifth the size of Brazil's. Two salaries close in dollars can rest on wage floors far apart.

Australia's prime minister and the U.S. president each collect more than three times Brazil's dollar sum, at US$433,900 and US$400,000. Canada's prime minister brings in about US$305,300, some two and a half times the Brazilian amount. All three trail Brazil on the ratio, with multiples of 12, 27, and 11.5. Europe sharpens the contrast. Ireland's Taoiseach posts the highest European multiple at nine, and Brazil's figure exceeds triple that level.

The Americas hold the widest gaps. Brazil, the U.S., and Mexico account for the three largest multiples, at 29, 27, and 25. Mexico's president outearns Brazil's in dollars, at about US$157,100 with benefits included, yet falls behind on the ratio. Mexico's figure also counts benefits, so Brazil's edge on the ratio survives against a broader measure of pay. Neto notes that some Latin American countries beyond these 10 show a wider gap. Brazil's top office looks modest to anyone tallying dollars and lavish to anyone earning the legal minimum, a split wider than any other leader's on the list.

Spain's president of the government received €95,944 in 2025, about US$107,300, the smallest dollar sum attached to any of the 10 leaders on the list.

Spain's salary trails the leaders above it by a wide margin. In dollars, it comes to about one-quarter of the Australian prime minister's pay and less than one-third of the U.S. president's federal salary. Brazil's president, the nearest leader in dollar terms, collects about US$13,400 more.

Four leaders on the list draw pay in euros, which strips exchange rates out of the comparison. Spain's €95,944 sits about €29,300 below the €125,220 Italy's prime minister receives from her parliamentary seat. France's president grosses €192,477 a year, about double the Spanish figure. Ireland's Taoiseach collects €256,311, more than two and a half times as much. Spain's leader is the only one of the four paid less than €100,000.

Spain's leader also sits closer to the country's lowest-paid full-time workers than any other leader with a minimum wage comparison, at 5.6 times the local minimum wage. Neto pairs Spain with the U.K. as the two countries showing the narrowest gaps, putting both at around 6 to 7 times. Britain's prime minister lands at 7 times, France's president at 8.6, and Ireland's Taoiseach at 9.

Brazil's president stands more than five times as far from that country's wage floor as Spain's leader does. Mexico's president sits nearly four and a half times as far. The U.S. president, at 27 times, stands nearly five times as far.

No other leader lands at the same end of both scales. Australia's prime minister collects the most in dollars, yet three other leaders show a wider gap to their own minimum wage. Brazil's president sits ninth in dollar terms despite the widest gap. Spain's head of government stays at the bottom on either yardstick, which makes the post the most modest on the list measured against foreign peers and against Spanish workers alike.

#5576. Five9 buys contact center intelligence startup Level AI after posting narrow earnings beat

Contact center company Five9 Inc. flexed its acquisitive muscles today as it announced a $325 million all-cash deal to buy an artificial intelligence-native rival called Level AI as it posted its third-quarter financial results.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Five9 is a leading player in the cloud contact center software industry, selling tools and services that enterprises use to manage their customer service interactions. Its web-based software spans traditional phone calls, video calls, emails, messaging, social media and other channels.

As for Level AI, it’s the developer of a contact center and customer experience intelligence platform that uses artificial intelligence to support human agents on calls and analyze, score and augment their interactions with the callers they serve. Its platform is designed to listen into customer service agent’s calls, so it can provide real-time guidance throughout and support workflow automation. The insights it generates can also be used to assist in agent coaching.

Level AI also develops autonomous AI agents that can automate some simpler customer inquiries and background operational tasks, freeing up human agents to focus on more complex customer issues. “Level AI’s AI applications help organizations improve agent performance, automate more customer interactions across voice and digital channels, and turn conversations into insights the whole organization can use,” Five9 said in a blog post announcing the deal. “Its applications are in production with enterprise customers today and handle more than 1 billion customer interactions a year.”

Five9 said it intends to continue offering Level AI’s applications as standalone tools for organizations that don’t want to shift their on-premises contact center operations to the cloud, also those who are using other cloud contact center platforms. However, it also plans to integrate the startup’s tools with its Genius CX Platform.

“As AI reshapes the customer experience landscape, we believe adding Level AI strengthens our competitive position, expands the customers we can serve, and deepens the AI talent behind our continuous innovation,” said Five9 Chief Executive Amit Mathradas.

Level AI founder and CEO Ashish Nagar said that by joining Five9, his company will be able to bring its applications and customer service-native AI models to thousands of new contact centers around the world, while allowing it to continue supporting its existing customers.

Investors don’t seem to have shared the CEOs’ enthusiasm for the deal, however, for Five9’s stock fell more than 23% in late trading after the deal was announced. That may be because of the cost of the acquisition. The $325 million cash outlay amounts to almost half of Five9’s current cash and marketable investments, which stood at $738 million at the end of the third quarter.

Five9’s results weren’t too bad. The company reported adjusted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $323.3 million, surpassing Wall Street’s guidance of 80 cents per share in earnings and $318.3 million in sales. But it’s notable that the company’s full-year guidance excludes any contributions from the pending deal, and so its value hinges on Five9’s ability to rapidly integrate Level AI’s technology.

For the current quarter, Five9 said it’s expecting earnings of between 88 and 92 cents per share on sales of $328 million to $334 million. But that guidance was mixed. Wall Street is looking for significantly higher earnings of 99 cents per share and $330.7 million in revenue.

For the full year, Five9 said it’s looking for earnings of $3.17 to $3.21 per share on total sales of $1.27 billion. Wall Street wants to see higher earnings of $3.26 per share on similar revenue.
