#5551. Buyers Stopped Believing Pitches. Give Them Something They Can Verify.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Software now writes the pitch, sends it and even personalizes it, so buyers have learned to discount all of it. Here’s what works now.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Anyone can write a good pitch now. A decent cold email, a tidy case study, a landing page full of confident claims. It takes a tool and about 10 minutes. Software now sends the outreach too, in volumes no person could match. Even the personal touches are written by it.

Buyers know all of this, and they have adjusted. The businesses winning new customers right now stopped asking to be believed and started letting people check.

Think about what a pitch actually is. It is the seller describing their own work in the best possible light. That was always a little suspect. Now it is also free to produce at scale, which means every competitor sounds equally polished and equally sure of themselves.

Buyers have noticed. The TrustRadius 2026 B2B Buying Disconnect report surveyed 1,862 technology buyers in January 2026. Among the buyers who used AI during their purchase, 94% fact-checked its answers at least some of the time. They are not only doubting vendors anymore. They are doubting the tools they use to research vendors.

The same report found that 74% of buyers use reviews to inform their decisions, and 83% shortlisted three or fewer products. Put those together. Buyers check outside sources, then narrow the field fast. If your claims can’t survive that check, you are out before the first conversation. The survey covers technology buyers, but the habit will sound familiar to anyone who sells anything.

The obvious fix is personalization. Mention the buyer’s recent post or their funding round or their new job. For a while, that worked, because it showed someone had paid attention.

It doesn’t show that anymore. When software writes the first line too, a personal detail only proves the sender has a decent data source. Most of us have received enough of these to spot the pattern, and a pattern with your name filled in is still a pattern.

A Gartner survey of about 645 B2B buyers, run in August and September 2025, found that 67% prefer a buying experience without a sales rep. A second release from the same survey found that 69% prefer to check AI-generated insights with a sales rep.

Those sound opposed, but they say one thing. Buyers want to evaluate on their own first, then talk to a person who will stand behind the answer. A cold email that asks for 15 minutes gives them neither.

Here is the version I would use. It rests on one idea. When words are cheap, the only signal left is effort the buyer can see.

Lead with something they can judge in under a minute. Skip the request for a meeting. Send a marked-up version of their landing page, a one-page teardown of their pricing or a short sample made from their own material. They should be able to evaluate it without replying, booking or talking to anyone.

Software can fake this, too. Marketer Dennis Yu described getting a seven-page AI-written audit in a cold email, with no real headlines or screenshots and a case study he says was made up. He saw through it. So give the buyer a way to tell. Real work names something only someone who looked would know. It includes one concrete fix. The buyer can check it in a minute. A named person will answer questions about it.

Send fewer. When tools make volume free, volume stops meaning anything. I would rather reach 20 prospects I studied than 2,000 I scraped. And put a person behind the follow-up. Reply fast and in your own words. Answer the hard question directly.

That advice is for cold outreach. Once you have paying customers, the free version runs into a different problem, and I learned it the hard way.

In my business, new clients could get one edited video before paying anything. When we started, 91.5% of trials turned into clients. We had fewer leads then and more time to focus on each one. Over the years, we added real clients, and their work came first. Trial edits got harder to fit in, and conversion dropped to 67%.

So we started charging a small fee for a single video. We also put a short fit call in front of it. Conversion from paid trial to customer is back to around 87%.

My read is that free work doesn’t scale because it competes with paid work for the same people’s time. A small fee pays for that time, so the trial gets the same attention as everything else. It also signals that the buyer is serious. They still judge real work before they commit, which was the point all along.

You don’t need a video for this. A small paid audit or a one-page plan works the same way. Keep it small enough that you can afford to do it often. And set the next step before you send anything, whether that is a call, a quote or a start date. A sample with no next step is a favor and not a sales process.

Anyone can write a good pitch now. A decent cold email, a tidy case study, a landing page full of confident claims. It takes a tool and about 10 minutes. Software now sends the outreach too, in volumes no person could match. Even the personal touches are written by it.

Buyers know all of this, and they have adjusted. The businesses winning new customers right now stopped asking to be believed and started letting people check.

Think about what a pitch actually is. It is the seller describing their own work in the best possible light. That was always a little suspect. Now it is also free to produce at scale, which means every competitor sounds equally polished and equally sure of themselves.

"Our goal is to expand access as much as possible in the different channels, knowing where consumers are and meeting them where they are," he said. Yuffa also told Bloomberg that patients on Hims & Hers previously had to go elsewhere to obtain Lilly's drugs, an extra step that deterred many of them from beginning treatment.

In its forward-looking statement, Hims & Hers cited the timing and logistics of integrating and rolling out Lilly medications on its platform as a risk, along with its ability to perform under the agreement on pricing and fulfillment.

#5549. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

GM's CFO sees a possible $2 billion cost headwind in 2027, while Ford's 2026 outlook assumes commodity headwinds near $2.5 billion

General Motors $GM and Ford $F Motor flagged rising costs as a risk to earnings growth in 2027 when they reported third-quarter results in October.

GM CFO Paul Jacobson said it is too early to issue an official 2027 forecast. He said inflation-driven expenses could again squeeze the automaker by $2 billion in 2027, matching the pressure it anticipates this year, according to CNBC. #5547. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Humana $HUM raised its full-year adjusted earnings guidance to at least $9.50 a share from at least $9.00 on Friday after third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $41.16 billion from $32.65 billion a year earlier, the company said.

The benefit ratio for the insurance segment, which measures medical costs as a share of premiums, was 93.7%, up from 91.1% a year earlier. That was better than management's guidance of slightly above 94%. The consolidated benefit ratio was 93.9%, compared with 91.1%.

Humana attributed the increase to the Star Ratings revenue headwind, higher benefit ratios among new individual Medicare Advantage members and smaller favorable reserve development from prior periods. That development was $67 million in the quarter, compared with $275 million a year earlier.

"Humana is delivering positive results for our members, our patients and their health," President and CEO Jim Rechtin said in a statement. "We are also increasingly driving financial and operating performance toward being 'ahead' of our plan," Rechtin said.

#5544. Kickstarter’s CEO is championing human creativity in a flood of AI

Good morning. Is Gen Z helping to create an economy of affection here in the U.S.? I first heard that term as a student at the University of Nairobi, when a classmate had to host a relative stranger in her apartment for two months because this person came from her village. As she explained to me, that’s just what you did. In a society without deep pockets, social programs, or job security, the bonds of community, kinship, religion, and tribe created a network of support.

My son, 25, calls it the friendship economy: he’ll buy t-shirts and go to concerts for a friend in music, help with another friend’s startup or movie, or sometimes throw a little money into various projects through some peer-to-peer platform. As AI and an anemic job market spark anxiety about traditional career paths, entrepreneurial and creative pursuits—sometimes funded by one’s social network—become more attractive. Goldman Sachs projects the number of creators to grow from 67 million to 107 million by 2030 and the creator economy to generate half a trillion dollars by next year.

I recently spoke with Kickstarter CEO Everette Taylor about how these trends are playing out on his crowdsourcing platform, which enabled more than 24 million backers to spend close to $9 billion in funding 277,302 projects as of April 2025, creating more than 1 million jobs. (Kickstarter launched in 2009 and became a public benefit corporation six years later.) Taylor says there’s one factor that’s both a catalyst and a challenge in the creator space: AI.

“It leads them to being a creator or entrepreneur, which also leads more people to our platform,” said Taylor. But he’s unnerved by what the technology can create on its own, telling me that he asked ChatGPT to produce a script about a “Mosquito Man” from the Bronx and “it gave me a full film script. It was insane.”

AI can write the script. What it can’t manufacture is the circle of people willing to back you, so Taylor is leaning into the human side of the equation.

Kickstarter cohosted a special event with smart projector brand XGIMI yesterday in Times Square, showcasing technology launched on the platform, including XGIMI’s new AURA 3 laser TV that raised a record $10 million in two hours. The goal was not just to promote the product but to create a sense of community, reinforcing Kickstarter’s brand campaign that kicked off this summer with the tagline “belief is human.”

“You go around Times Square and what do you see? Nothing but AI, AI, AI ads,” said Taylor. But on his platform, backers seem to be voting the other way. One 2026 study tracked 63,000 Kickstarter campaigns and found projects with the “AI use” label raised about 40% less money and drew almost a quarter fewer backers. People want to know they’re supporting human-generated work and the human behind it.

“We believe in the importance of human creativity no matter how much AI advances things,” said Taylor, who launched a $1 million Kickstarter Culture Fund to help independent creators make a living. “I don’t care if you have a million followers on social media. Those 25,000 people that you have on Kickstarter, those are your true supporters.”Contact CEO Daily via Diane Brady at diane.brady@fortune.com

The tech stocks have their worst day since 2025

The midterm hangover hit tech hard. Two days after voters turned against AI data centers, the Nasdaq sank more than 5% on Thursday, its steepest drop since April 2025’s tariff shock, while chipmakers Micron and AMD each fell about 14%. Elon Musk, who spent hundreds of millions backing Republicans, took a big personal hit: Tesla and SpaceX shed about $456 billion in two days, cutting his fortune by roughly $113 billion.

The Iran war has cost U.S. households nearly $2,000—and the bill is still rising

The war in the Middle East has cost the average U.S. household nearly $2,000, according to an estimate by Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi. Further strikes could push that bill higher.

Vietnam’s state-owned oil and gas giant briefly lost access to Middle Eastern crude after Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz, CEO Le Manh Cuong says. Now, Petrovietnam is investing in LNG, offshore wind, and nuclear power to meet the country’s growing energy needs.

#5542. Is Trump Media Selling Bitcoin? Democrats Prepare Crypto Probe

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Trump Media has moved $343 million in Bitcoin to Crypto.com, raising fresh questions if Donald Trump’s media company could be selling its crypto holdings. The transfer comes as Democrats prepare investigations into Trump’s family crypto ventures following their midterm election victories.

The company sent 4,259 BTC in two transactions, according to blockchain data tracked by Arkham. The coins came from wallets labeled as collateral for convertible notes, adding another layer of uncertainty around the Trump Media Bitcoin transfer.

The timing is difficult to ignore. Trump Media faces a potential $1 billion debt repayment deadline later this month, while incoming Democratic lawmakers are preparing to scrutinize Trump’s crypto businesses. A sale has not been confirmed, but this move puts the company’s Bitcoin treasury under pressure.

Arkham data showed Trump Media-linked wallets transferring 4,259 BTC to Crypto.com just a few hours ago. The coins were moved in two batches of more than 2,000 BTC each. The transfer represents around $343 million at recent prices. It also accounts for 30% of the 14,139 BTC Trump Media previously held, including pledged coins.

However, the destination does not confirm a sale. It is known that Trump Media has used Crypto.com for custody and trading-related transfers before, including transactions in May and August.

The latest movement is particularly notable because the Bitcoin came from wallets associated with convertible-note collateral. Trump Media’s previous filings identified 4,260.73 BTC as collateral for its notes.

A November 2 filing also disclosed that noteholders can require cash repayment on November 30. If all eligible holders exercise that option, the company could face approximately $1 billion in repayments.

Trump Media warned that refinancing or other measures might not be sufficient. In that scenario, the company could be forced to sell Bitcoin or other digital assets to meet its obligations.

This disclosure gives the Crypto.com transfer a potentially more serious explanation than routine custody management. The company may be positioning assets ahead of a major liquidity decision. Although the reason remains unconfirmed, Trump Media could be selling its Bitcoin.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The transfer also arrives as Democrats prepare to investigate Trump’s family crypto businesses after winning control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Incoming lawmakers have identified World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture, as a potential focus. Investigators are expected to examine foreign investment, business profits, and possible conflicts of interest involving the administration’s crypto dealings.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 Democrats plan to investigate crypto industry's financial ties to President Trump and his family, Bloomberg reports. pic.twitter.com/KGF41xeknO

Senator Elizabeth Warren has pledged scrutiny of Trump’s crypto business relationships, while Representative Robert Garcia, expected to lead House Oversight, warned Trump-linked interests to prepare for investigations.

Democrats are expected to gain subpoena power when the new Congress begins in January. Reuters previously reported that investigations into Trump family businesses could begin as early as February.

The current political environment could complicate the outlook for Trump-linked companies. Congressional scrutiny may increase pressure on financial relationships, crypto holdings, and business operations connected to the president’s family.

So, is Trump Media selling its Bitcoin? There’s no clarity as of now, but a confirmed sale would raise questions if Trump Media is reducing its crypto treasury to meet financial obligations.

The next major date is November 30, when noteholders can exercise their repayment option. Investors will also be watching if the Bitcoin remains at Crypto.com, moves again, or appears in transactions that indicate an actual sale.

#5541. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5540. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5539. Your customers are lying to you, and they’re lying to themselves too

Sam Peskin is the co-founder and CEO of Early Studies, a research and innovation partner to brands and policymakers. Anyone, the startup described in this piece, was run by his Early Studies co-founder, Alfred Malmros.

One little white lie at a time, some of the world’s biggest businesses are being undone by bad consumer data, and they don’t know it yet. Now that new tools like synthetic audiences are being thrown into the mix, the boardroom faces a novel problem.

Let’s start at the beginning. It doesn’t take a genius to know that businesses need good data to understand their consumers. To market effectively, brands need to know what their audiences are thinking, feeling and doing.

For almost 20 years, I’ve advised brands on how to and how not to connect with young audiences through “culture.” Working at VICE at the height of its influence, our job when we walked into the boardroom was essentially to scare the living daylights out of senior marketing execs, who had no idea about the attitudes, behaviors, tastes and desires that defined the young people they were trying to talk to. Working with us was the only way they would save themselves from certain death.

Millennials were shaped by the pillars of their parents’ realities crumbling around them. That this would in fact become the mood music for the next two decades was at the time unknown. But the lack of accurate data available to decision-makers to educate themselves was itself what provided the opportunity for VICE to flourish.

Fast forward 15 years and much remains the same. Big brands are drowning in lines of consumer data they have little use for, and their competitors are acting on the same generic narratives as them. Legacy polling companies have always told brands X percent of people think Y about their product. They ask direct, generic questions and they get direct, generic answers. These answers become polemic (for want of anything more interesting or, dare to say it, insightful) and the world keeps on spinning.

It might seem like a small, or even interpersonal, problem. But brands regularly build multimillion-dollar projects on the backs of the lies people tell about themselves. Serious money is going to the wrong places: a study last year by the research organization Esomar estimated the “insights industry” was worth $150 billion, with $56 billion spent on market research alone. How many of the people holding these budgets would tell you that they are getting full value for their money (and have accurate data to back this up)?

My co-founder, Alfred Malmros, is among those stung. He ran a startup called Anyone, an app that provided five-minute advice calls from anyone in the world. Like all responsible founders, he wanted to figure out whether people wanted what he was building and launched a product-market-fit survey. The results filled him with confidence that everyone wanted it.

That prediction didn’t wash with the download statistics, which peaked at 25,000 and dwindled to 1,000 active users over time. The same people who claimed they would love an on-call advice service never downloaded the app. It was this painful lesson that taught us that the wrong questions generate the wrong answers.

If my co-founder had known at the time why we lie and how lies fuel bad data, the crisis could have been averted.

Picture this. You’re at a dinner party with a half dozen people you don’t know that well. The conversation is about climate change and the scale of the challenge it presents to humankind. Everyone concurs: It’s a big one.

A guest has just finished saying that climate change keeps her up at night, to thoughtful nods from the rest of the table, and then she turns to you and says: What do you think?

In the moment most of us would agree. It would take a contrarian to take a different or contradictory position. Or even to admit that, honestly, what actually kept us up at night was our mortgage or the dreaded monthly 1:1 with our manager the next day.

There are countless examples of this with brands: Ask people why they want an expensive watch, and they will say the craftsmanship; ask them why others want one, and they will say status.

Whether conscious or not, we so often default to dishonesty. We lie to make sense of ourselves to others, to make sense of a world that is increasingly nonsensical. It’s not a moral failing, but it is a sticky conundrum for the businesses trying to understand us.

The first solution is simple: Ask people what their friends think. Academics have shown that when people answer questions on behalf of their social circle instead of themselves, they effectively report on many people beyond themselves, which tells us a lot more about society than a direct question to one person.

Second, stop asking people what they think only in that moment, and broaden it to what they’ve already experienced and what they expect to experience. Ask the same question about five years ago, today and three years from now and you’ll get back data on the direction of travel in beliefs and behavior, not just a snapshot.

My business partner and I built our research consultancy on these parameters. Consumer data sets are so often made up of people’s projections and manifestations, the ways in which they’d like to be seen. To get to real truths, even better, hidden truths, researchers must solve for this.

Even better, design for it. When enough intelligence (human or artificial, ideally a blend of both) goes into crafting a question, the question itself is enough to unlock new futures and opportunities, and for those who ask the question to see their worlds anew.

Because bad data alone isn’t a new problem. It’s been compounded by the rise of synthetic audiences: AI-generated simulations of real consumers that businesses can interview and test ideas on before launching them.

In theory it’s useful, but when these audiences are trained on flawed consumer data, the consequences are catastrophic.

If businesses aren’t paying attention to the nature of the data going into these models, the results may look good, but they will be fundamentally inaccurate. It’s a problem we’re already seeing play out. Taking a broken methodology and feeding it bad data will only make the wrong answers arrive faster.

With or without AI acceleration, if more businesses knew how to ask consumers the right questions, we would break the cycle of bad data and bad decisions that has existed for decades, averting C-suite crises. The companies that continue to solve for an imagined version of their consumer will lose to the companies solving for the real one.

#5538. AI won’t pay off for the S&P 493 until CEOs rebuild the work

Adam Dumey leads enterprise frontier lab strategy at World Wide Technology (WWT), a privately held technology firm. WWT sells the enterprise AI integration work this piece recommends and partners with NVIDIA, Dell, Cisco and Microsoft. He holds no positions in the companies mentioned.

Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok wrote on Oct. 24 that outside the technology sector, AI has delivered zero financial payoff. Revenue per worker and profit margins are rising at the Magnificent 7 and flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Outside tech, he writes, token spending is a cost center weighing on margins. The AI story “will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7.”

Slok has the beneficiaries right. Thus far, the value has sat with the companies selling AI infrastructure, not the enterprises consuming the technology. The Oct. 28 earnings reports made the point: for the quarter ended Sept. 30, Azure revenue grew 48% and Google Cloud 103%, driven in large part by AI demand. The buyers of that capacity reported job cuts, not margin gains. The more interesting discussion is what is happening inside those companies that keeps their spend from converting to realized gains, what has to change, and when it will.

Surveys this year from the St. Louis Fed and the Census Bureau put work use of generative AI at about 40% of workers and adoption at about a quarter of firms. Individuals are running ahead of their employers. Employees are saving real hours with AI. Some teams, and sometimes whole divisions, are seeing real benefit too. But those gains are not adding up across the enterprise, because the core operating model has not changed. The workflows, the processes and the decision approvals were built around people doing the work, and the reviews, handoffs and sign-offs are still there even after AI has taken over the task. In an AI-enabled operation, a process built for human pacing becomes the constraint, which is why the gains stay in pockets instead of reaching the whole company.

Executives nod at “operating model.” Boards ask what it means in practice. Three things rise to the surface, and each is hard to enact in the companies Slok is describing.

First, AI must be a CEO-owned initiative. That does not mean sponsorship. It means one accountable party for building a new operating system and making the difficult calls that come with it: declaring the outcome, setting the pace, redesigning the work, deciding how much trust to extend to a model, and choosing what gets measured. Nobody below the CEO carries the same authority to enforce those decisions in every function. The most common pattern I see in enterprises not realizing value is the opposite of ownership: the CEO has delegated AI to IT or a transformation office, approved a budget, and is waiting for a result that the organization has no mandate to produce.

Second, picking the right problems and rebuilding the work around them. The filter is whether a workflow is material, not whether it is interesting: does it move revenue, margin, risk or cycle time, and will one business leader own the outcome. Pass that filter and the hard work begins: deconstructing workflows to eliminate dated processes, redefining roles so that work once performed, reviewed and approved by people alone is shared with AI without losing accountability, resetting approval authorities to the point where judgment is now applied, and establishing a governance model that operates at runtime, because AI produces output at a volume and speed that no manual review can keep pace with. That is where most of the time goes.

Third, the AI itself. Slok is right that most companies do not need the latest model, and enterprises increasingly understand that. Less understood are the layers beneath that conversation. Start with whether an AI model is needed at all: significant improvements are available through deterministic automation that most organizations have never pursued, while many are using frontier models for routine tasks. Then comes infrastructure. Increasingly I am discussing the optimal mix of open and closed models, which revives the considerations of the cloud versus on-premises era with one difference: cloud took a decade to become multi-cloud, and model strategy is multi-vendor from the start. Finally, selecting a model is not a one-time event. That capability is very rare in most organizations today.

None of this is a technology project. It touches every function and lives inside core processes.

Boards then ask how long. Every executive team reaches the same realization: this is more expensive than we thought. Not because of token prices but because the build costs more than it returns until it is done. BCG’s Applied AI Index puts AI spending at 3.3% of revenue now, up from 1.7% in late 2025. That is Slok’s cost center, seen from the inside.

The temptation is to skip the build and cut staff. Barclays announced roughly 5,000 job cuts on Oct. 22 and cited AI, and markets read it as the payoff arriving. Barclays’ own chief executive called AI “the icing on the cake,” and the bank has not said how much of the number is attributable to AI at all.

The right number has two sides. On one, the quality of the outcome: did the work meet the KPI or service level the business set for it. On the other, the full cost of producing it: the model, the data, the orchestration, the validation, the human handling of exceptions, the rework and the governance, of which token spend is one line and rarely the largest. Enterprise AI will be measured this way, paying for outcomes accepted rather than intelligence consumed, and almost no company can produce that number today. Their dashboards show what is being used, by model, and nothing about what that spend returned. So the bill arrives before the value does, and the market reads layoffs instead.

Given the ownership, redesign and measurement work still ahead at most companies, I would not expect widespread acknowledgement of specific, measurable AI benefits before the end of 2027. Widespread gains across the 493 are at least a couple of years away.

Until then, four questions tell you where your company stands:

Slok’s flat line is the average of 493 answers to those questions. It will move when the answers do.

#5537. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

Partisanship has weakened the institutions of U.S. democracy (“independent judiciary, impartial bureaucracy, control of corruption”) ever since President Clinton and House Speaker Newt Gingrich clashed in the 1990s, they say. As evidence, they cite the U.S. slipping down Transparency International’s corruption index:

But after the Great Financial Crisis of 2008, “the conservative SCOTUS turned activist” and began eroding congressional oversight. At the same time, “SCOTUS has not only granted virtual immunity to the president, but also eliminated the century-old tradition of independent civil service, including independent agencies: all now serve at the president's pleasure. The only partial exception was granted to the Fed.”

The result is that “SCOTUS appears to be restructuring institutions around a generic future elected monarchy, with only three truly independent pillars: the president, SCOTUS and Fed.”

Can the nation be saved? Yes, they say, “if Republicans descend into civil war, survival instincts may kick in, creating a bipartisan coalition that might push through middle-of-the-road bills addressing some of these issues. “Thus, the proverbial ‘self-correcting’ nature of the U.S. might work again,” they wrote, “But it won't be easy.”

The carnage may be about to end: Nasdaq futures were up 1.18% this morning before the open in New York. S&P 500 futures were up 0.24%. Traders seem to be signaling that the massive selloff in tech stocks over the last 24 hours may be overdone.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% yesterday, and the index is firmly in correction territory. The S&P was down more than 4%—a huge step down for the blue chip index. More than $3 trillion in market cap was lost. Twenty-two Asian billionaires lost $18 billion of their net worth, Bloomberg calculated.

But as dawn breaks over the Eastern Seaboard in America, there are signs of light at the end of the tunnel. In addition to futures rising, non-tech stocks have proven resilient, according to Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank:

“The rotation trade [out of tech stocks] over the last month has had a profound impact with S&P’s information technology (-15.89%) and communication services (-13.43%) posting sharp losses, whereas consumer staples (+13.96%) and healthcare (+11.24%) have posted equally sharp gains. #5535. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

#5534. JPMorgan’s M&A chief sees softer 2027–but a potential upside surprise in private equity exits

Morgan Chittum here. Private equity firms have spent years waiting for a better time to sell. By the second half of 2027, some may have to stop waiting.

That’s the view of Charlie Bouckaert, JPMorgan’s global head of M&A. He expects sponsors to start moving towards liquidity—not because he sees a dealmaking boom ahead, but because they’re running out of reasons to put it off. Their holdings are getting older, refinancing deadlines are approaching, and investors want their money back.

“Ultimately, the private equity business model is reliant on exiting and returning capital to LPs,” Bouckaert told me. “And so that’s going to have to happen.”

After all, backlogs are massive and growing. Private equity inventory of unsold investments hit 33,853 as of Sept. 30, 2026, up from 33,575 at the end of June, according to PitchBook figures reported by the Wall Street Journal. At the current pace of exits, PitchBook estimates it would take more than eight years to clear that inventory.

This is, in part, a byproduct of private equity’s natural boom-and-bust cycle. A record-setting 2021 made way for sharp slowdown as aggressive interest rate hikes in 2022 ended the cheap-debt era. The recovery ever since then has been uneven. Although deal and exit values rebounded in 2025, the industry entered 2026 with roughly 32,000 unsold companies. Buyout holding periods have stretched to around seven years, compared with five to six years between 2010 and 2021, according to Bain.

“You have a number of assets that have been held for a long period of time,” Bouckaert said.

Some of those companies could also need to refinance in 2028 or 2029. As those deadlines get closer, private equity firms will have to decide whether to sell or keep holding—and how to finance those businesses if they do. “The more imminent nature of that is going to force a more definitive evaluation of what to do next,” he added.

Still, Bouckaert’s private equity forecast isn’t a call for a broader M&A surge. After what he described as a “very, very robust environment in 2026,” particularly during the first two-thirds of the year, dealmaking hit a lull. Activity remains relatively healthy, but Bouckaert expects 2027 to look more like the recent stretch than those earlier highs.

“We expect the composition of [the market] to continue to skew towards larger deals the way that it has, but there to be slightly fewer of those,” he said, pointing to AI-related mergers and acquisitions.

And for private equity firms, returning money to investors won’t always mean selling a company outright. “The exact format in which it happens may change,” Bouckaert said. “Maybe it’s a continuation fund. Maybe it’s the structure of a secondary deal.”

Continuation funds let sponsors move investments into a new vehicle they also manage, giving existing investors a chance to cash out. Investors can also sell their stakes to new buyers through the secondary market.

“But one way or another, we do expect to see greater deal flow materialize there,” he said.

#5533. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5532. Schellman CEO: the giant loophole in the White House AI deal

The White House recently brought together some of the world’s largest AI companies around an important commitment: independent oversight of the safeguards designed to keep their systems safe. The accord, released on Sept. 29, calls on developers to monitor risks, establish internal controls and bring in outside auditors or evaluators to assess whether those controls work. It’s an encouraging development for an industry where companies have largely been responsible for evaluating their own technology.

But the agreement leaves a critical gap. It calls for independent assessments without defining who qualifies to conduct them, what independence requires or how conflicts of interest should be handled. Without those standards, two developers could fulfill the same commitment through assessments with vastly different levels of rigor and objectivity, leaving businesses and regulators uncertain about how much confidence to place in the results.

Consider an AI developer hiring a firm to evaluate its safety controls. The evaluator agrees to a narrow scope, performs testing and issues a favorable report. If that same firm helped design the controls under review, its objectivity deserves scrutiny. If major risks fall outside the scope, customers might mistake limited findings for a broader endorsement of the system.

For executives choosing AI vendors, these distinctions shape purchasing and deployment decisions. They need to know who performed the assessment, whether they had the right expertise, which safeguards they examined and what they excluded. The evaluator also needs access to sufficient evidence and the freedom to report unfavorable findings. A report is useful only when readers understand both its conclusions and its limits.

Assessors should disclose relevant commercial relationships before work begins and document how they manage conflicts. They should use defined criteria, explain their methods and face independent quality review. Accreditation, where appropriate, adds another way to verify competence and impartiality.

The real test of independent oversight comes when an assessment uncovers something a developer would rather not hear. The accord calls for internal teams to address identified risks, with an independent board committee overseeing findings and responses. But those safeguards depend on assessors having the independence to report concerns without pressure to soften their conclusions.

Consider an evaluator who identifies a serious cybersecurity vulnerability in a frontier model. If the developer disputes the finding or pushes to narrow its scope, the evaluator must be able to stand behind the evidence and communicate the risk clearly. The developer then needs to determine whether additional testing, corrective action or release restrictions are warranted. Without an independent assessment that accurately captures the original risk, even a well-defined remediation process can fall short.

Credible AI assurance also requires the right expertise. Technical evaluators understand model behavior, emerging capabilities and attack scenarios, while assurance professionals bring experience evaluating governance, internal controls and supporting evidence. Both perspectives are necessary, but neither automatically qualifies someone to assess every aspect of an AI system. As AI assurance evolves, the industry needs clearer expectations for the qualifications, methodologies and oversight required of those conducting assessments.

We’re already seeing progress in how AI assurance is conducted. The AICPA and AIUC recently announced a joint offering pairing SOC 2 examinations with AIUC-1 certification, combining established assurance practices with technical testing of AI agents, including quarterly retesting as risks evolve. It’s a promising step toward more rigorous assessments, but stronger methodologies alone cannot guarantee credible results. The assessors applying them must also demonstrate the expertise, independence and accountability necessary to earn trust.

The companies signing the accord have an opportunity to establish clearer expectations for independent AI assurance. That should include minimum qualifications for assessors, transparent assessment methodologies, conflict-of-interest disclosures and independent quality oversight. Reports should clearly communicate their scope, limitations and material findings so boards, regulators and customers can understand what was evaluated and how much confidence to place in the results.

Standards also need to be practical for smaller developers. AI adoption extends beyond the largest technology companies, and an assurance process so expensive that smaller firms cannot participate would leave gaps across the market. Expectations should match the risks involved without compromising independence.

The White House has taken an important step by putting independent oversight at the center of its AI safety commitments. But for that oversight to carry weight, the industry needs clear standards for who can conduct assessments, how their independence is verified and what accountability looks like when those standards aren’t met. Without those expectations, developers may be able to demonstrate that an assessment took place without proving it was credible. As AI systems take on greater responsibility, the people evaluating them must be held to equally rigorous standards.

#5531. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”
