#5530. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

#5529. Canva Is Cutting Employees After Its ‘Hardest Year Yet.’ Here’s What Their Unusually ‘Generous’ Severance Packages Include.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Forget benefits that help you stay. This package is designed to help you move on.

You have just lost your job. Can your employer help you find the next one?

That’s the question thousands of workers face at Canva, a graphic design platform launched in 2013. This week, Canva said that it is laying off, changing roles or relocating 1,271 employees, or about 22% of its workforce.

The move is a major restructuring that arrives in the wake of Canva’s “hardest year yet,” according to a memo sent to employees by co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins. She mentioned that in the past year, the company’s growth slowed for the first time in 10 years.

“After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough,” Perkins wrote. “To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to re-found Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams.”

Perkins said that all affected employees will receive at least six months of pay regardless of where they live.

Typically, any equity Canva employees hold vests after a year with the company. However, laid-off workers will be eligible to keep their equity regardless of how long they’ve been with Canva.

Departing employees will also receive another 12 months of healthcare coverage in countries where Canva currently offers it, plus 12 months of access to its employee assistance program, Canva Care, for themselves and their families.

Canva’s approach reflects a broader shift toward more career support for departing employees, according to Greg Simpson, who leads the global career transition and mobility practice at talent advisory firm LHH.

“It does not surprise us to see an offer that’s like this,” Simpson said in a recent interview with Business Insider.

Canva is also offering individual coaching, interview preparation and a year of LinkedIn Premium to departing employees. The company is assigning a significant portion of its recruiting team to review resumes and practice interviews.

Employees can opt into an alumni talent directory that Canva will share with investors, partners and its wider industry network to help them find new roles. They can also keep their company MacBooks, because “we know not everyone has a personal laptop,” Perkins wrote in the memo.

The company is also putting money behind entrepreneurship. Through its new Canva Collective Fund, the company will offer $10,000 grants to departing employees who want to start a business or launch a community project. Anyone leaving as part of these changes has until December 14 to register interest. Canva will not take an ownership stake in anything they create.

Canva will keep Slack and Gmail open through the end of the week, giving affected employees time to absorb the news and say goodbye to colleagues on their own terms.

In an interview with Newsweek, KnotDating co-founder and CEO Jasveer Singh praised Canva’s handling of the layoffs, calling it “a master-class.”

He said the company’s announcement was “thoughtful, honest and generous.”

#5528. Current price of oil as of November 6, 2026

At 7:15 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil was priced at $102.05 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s an increase of $2.53 compared with yesterday morning and around $38 higher than the price one year ago.

It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast.

Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business.

Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.”

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas.

To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks:

Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5527. Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 8:04 amNovember 3, 2026 at 8:09 am

Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.

The change, announced Monday, opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.

For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.

Microsoft Foundry, the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.

The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.

Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000.

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules. To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.

The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.

#5526. Zillennials are ‘loud working ’: They’re spending 5 hours a week self-promoting themselves—and colleagues are getting so annoyed they’re quitting

So you’ve heard of the trend quiet quitting, and its sister, loud quitting—but now workers are doing the complete opposite: “loud working.” Instead of doing the bare minimum to get by or turning their anger on their employers, they’re pouring all their energy into making their work more visible.

Think of the colleague who posts every win on LinkedIn or pings the whole team on Slack the second a task is done.

New research from Tide, a finance platform, found that the average U.K. worker spends 131 hours a year—more than 17 working days or 2.8 hours a week—making their work visible. That includes singing their own praises on social media, posting updates on Slack or Teams, speaking up in meetings, and vocalizing their wins to anyone who will listen.

And the loudest of all are younger workers: In fact, nearly 70% of 25- to 34-year-olds are “loud working.” They’re spending about 5 hours every week self-promoting. And it’s drawing attention from management, clients and even angry coworkers.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, it’s not always the most competent worker who gets rewarded—it’s the one who makes the most noise about it.

According to the research, 77% of “loud workers” have had at least one career opportunity in the past year alone, including new customers or clients, pay rises and promotions. For 15% of respondents, getting vocal about their wins has even gotten them awards.

And all the new noise around their success is attracting the attention of other employers; In fact, 17% say they’ve not only been poached, but they’ve actually landed a new job because they’ve been more vocal about their work.

But worryingly, it’s not just “loud workers” who are at risk of being snapped up and leaving the business.

Not everyone’s cheering. More than one in four (27%) workers have considered leaving a job because of a loud working culture, or because colleagues are too vocal about their own achievements.

Zillennials are both most likely to be guilty of “loud working,” as well as the ones walking off.  They’re posting about their success at more than three times the rate of over-55s. Yet nearly half of 25 to 34-year-olds have considered quitting a job because of it—and one in five already have.

Some industries are more forgiving of office braggers than others: Workers in IT, telecoms, and finance are the most likely to have had enough of performative culture. Meanwhile, men are more likely than women to have already quit over it.

“Loudworking has mixed reactions in the workplace and it’s easy to understand that a colleague who turns every small win into an announcement might be off-putting,” said George Schmidt, Tide’s CEO for the U.K. and Europe. “But our research shows there’s a difference between being performative and backing yourself.”

He said that for small business owners, sharing their work, wins and expertise is often the most effective marketing they have. And the same goes for anyone who has left their employer to go solo or who is eyeing up the exit.

Ultimately, though, many workers want to be at a business that rewards people for actually doing the hard work—not just shouting the most about it.

Do you ‘loud work’—or have you quit over a colleague who does? Get in touch: orianna.royle@fortune.com

Orianna Rosa Royle is the Success associate editor at Fortune, overseeing careers, leadership, and company culture coverage. She was previously the senior reporter at Management Today, Britain's longest-running publication for CEOs.

#5525. Opinion: San Francisco is delivering, while Seattle is still deliberating

by Joe Nguyễn on Nov 3, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 3, 2026 at 9:47 am

Editor’s note: GeekWire publishes guest opinions to highlight a range of perspectives on issues shaping the tech and startup community. To submit a guest column, email [email protected].

How can a region care so much, spend billions in tax dollars and yet leave people losing faith in its future?

In Seattle, that question has become painfully familiar. People see suffering and disorder on their streets with little reason to believe help is coming. Business owners wonder whether the city values their presence or understands what it takes to keep their doors open. Even people who love this place are beginning to speak about its problems as permanent.

That growing resignation took us to San Francisco. We wanted to understand how a city so many had written off was giving people reasons to believe in its future again.

I expected to come home impressed with San Francisco. Instead, I came home with a deeper appreciation for Seattle. And an anger I am still trying to reconcile.

Seeing San Francisco make progress reminded me that Seattle has the talent and resources to do the same, perhaps even better. That is what made me frustrated. We should not have to accept people suffering on our streets and businesses struggling to stay open as conditions beyond our ability to change.

Not long ago, San Francisco had become a warning about what happens when a prosperous city loses its way. Less than two years into Mayor Daniel Lurie’s administration, that story has begun to change. Reported crime fell 22 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. According to Kidder Mathews, office vacancy declined to 26 percent in the third quarter from 31 percent in the prior year.

San Francisco still has profound problems, and the suffering we saw on its streets cannot be erased by encouraging statistics. But the people we met shared a confidence that their work could change the city’s direction. They understood what they were working toward and could explain what would happen next. Their optimism comes from seeing progress and believing they can build on it.

And I kept wondering why that felt so refreshing.

Seattle has extraordinary talent and resources, with public servants who care deeply and service providers doing demanding work under difficult conditions. Our business community helps shape the world. With that much ability and commitment here, we should feel confident that we can make our own neighborhoods safer and more welcoming.

Yet we often seem more resigned to our limitations than confident in our possibilities.

I recognize that habit because I have worked inside it. As a legislator and state agency director, I saw good intentions fall short when leaders avoided hard decisions and failed to hold people accountable for results. Even small obstacles became accepted excuses when no one took responsibility for overcoming them.

Throughout the trip, I kept looking for a more complicated explanation for the difference between San Francisco and Seattle. Eventually, the answer became impossible to miss.

Leaders expected the institutions they led to deliver results and took responsibility for making that happen. The unsettling part was how unfamiliar something so basic had come to feel.

San Francisco offered examples of what happens when leaders refuse to accept failure.

“Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.”

One example was Mayor Lurie’s response to open-air drug markets. The previous administration had already brought police, public health officials and other agencies together, but people we met described meetings that produced more updates than action. Lurie took that existing structure and gave it a clear purpose. Participants were expected to make decisions and take responsibility for carrying them out, then return with evidence of what had changed on the streets.

This approach helped illuminate a problem that is also familiar to Seattle. Officers encountering someone dangerously intoxicated often have no appropriate place to take them. Leaving the person on the street puts them and others at risk, while taking them to jail does little to address their need for care and would remove scarce law enforcement officials from patrol for hours.

San Francisco opened the RESET Center to fill this gap. Eligible individuals are able to receive brief medical supervision and stabilization, followed by connections to services. The center opened within ten months of the decision to proceed. It is a limited response to a larger crisis, but it gives people an option they lacked.

Across our conversations, leadership meant staying with a problem until the next step became possible. That requires something more uncomfortable than calling for accountability. It requires accepting that evidence may challenge an approach we have previously defended.

If we believe Seattle is a progressive city, we should ask whether our policies deliver the progress we promise. That means questioning our assumptions and changing programs when results fall short. Reconsidering an approach can feel like abandoning our values, but those values should compel us to change when people are still in need of help.

The business community must reconsider its own habits too. We often avoid politics even as public decisions shape our future. In San Francisco, business leaders helped set the agenda and backed leaders willing to act. If we want better outcomes here, we must help shape the decisions that produce them.

Government, in turn, must make clear that businesses belong here. A shop owner asking for a safe doorway and a person in crisis outside that door both deserve a response. A capable city should be able to care for both.

People form their judgment of a city through these encounters. They notice whether someone answers. They notice whether anything changes.

Over time, those experiences become confidence or despair.

San Francisco reminded me that resignation can lift. People can begin expecting more when they see reasons to believe their efforts matter.

Seattle has so much worth believing in. What we need is leadership willing to turn that promise into something people can feel.

Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.

What might we accomplish if we recovered it?

#5524. Tech Giants Are Putting Billions Behind a Decades-Old Engineering Model. Here’s Why It Matters More Now.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The FDE title might be new, but the theory is as old as computers themselves.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

If you’ve followed tech news this summer, you’ve almost certainly come across the term Forward Deployed Engineer or, in short, FDE. On June 30, AWS announced a massive $1 billion investment in a new unit built around this one role. OpenAI had already put more than $4 billion behind its own Deployment Company in May. There’s no end to the news on FDE. All of this for just one role.

So, who are they? A forward deployed engineer is an engineer embedded directly in a customer’s environment to design, build and ship AI or custom software solutions. Palantir, which made the title popular, describes the difference well. A regular engineer builds “one capability, many customers.” An FDE delivers “one customer, many capabilities.”

Companies have put engineers close to customers for decades. In the 1950s and 60s, IBM sent systems engineers to sit with customers alongside its mainframes, writing code and configuring the machine — all of it included in the price of the hardware until IBM started charging for it separately at the end of the 60s. Later, consultants embedded themselves inside client organizations, and implementation teams worked side by side with business users.

Because the way enterprise software gets built has changed, and the FDE is the role that fits the new way of building.

Across years, the best way to describe the business and IT relationship was like a client and vendor. Business teams gave the requirement. IT took that requirement and took six months, sometimes a year, with large teams across development, integration, testing and training for a project.

A lot got lost along the way. What the business wrote and what IT understood were rarely the same thing, and that gap only showed up in testing, the most expensive place to find it. And because IT built it and IT ran it, the business never really owned it. Every small change went back into the queue. This is the gap between a solution being “deployed” and being “valuable.”

But now, with AI-assisted coding, or vibe coding, a business user can put together a first working version of an app in days. It won’t be production-ready, but it’s real enough to show what they mean instead of describing it in a document.

That changes the order of things. The process doesn’t have to be frozen before you automate it. You can reimagine the process while you build, because trying an idea now costs a few days, not a quarter.

But this first-version app lacks the practical connect to the data or the information that another team has. It doesn’t pass a security review. It doesn’t scale. Someone has to take what the business already knows it wants and turn it into something the enterprise can actually run.

So, the hard part is no longer just building the technology. It is getting technology, data, workflows and people to work together in a way that changes an outcome. That too, quickly. That requires a different form of accountability.

A true FDE is an engineer first. They write production code, they work inside the customer’s data and systems, and they ship. Someone who writes a strategy deck under a new title is a consultant.

Engineering depth or technical depth: SQL, cloud, Python and real experience putting LLMs and agents into production. They need to understand the ins and outs of governance, security and compliance.

Functional knowledge: Doesn’t mean you need doctors to work in pharma and life sciences projects. For example, OpenAI’s healthcare FDE role asks for experience with payer workflows, provider operations, EHR systems or standards like HL7 and FHIR, and the ability to “translate payer, provider or health-system workflows into technical requirements and measurable outcomes.” The same posting says clinical credentials are not required.

So functional knowledge here means three things. Knowing how work actually moves through the function: who approves what, where the handoffs are, where it breaks. Knowing the systems and data that function runs on. And knowing the rules it operates under. An FDE in healthcare billing needs different context from one in supply chain. What they don’t need is to be the subject matter expert. They need to sit with one and ask the right questions.

Discovery and judgment: As per my experience with FDEs, they’re spending roughly 60%-70% of their time with the customer. They need to scope problems that come with no spec and explain technical trade-offs in business terms.

Outcome ownership: The roles that pay a premium are tied to customer outcomes, not tickets closed. Let’s go back to the IBM systems engineer era. The outcome there was “Did we deploy the system successfully?” and that’s it. Now it has changed to “Did the system create measurable value?” — essentially owning the business outcome.

And the team is lean. Inside an enterprise, the way we’d staff it is two or three engineers, someone from the business who knows the function inside out, someone accountable for data and the platform, and a business owner who holds the metric.

This is the question I get most from CIOs. If a small team is building fast with the business, what stops it from becoming shadow IT with better branding?

A true FDE team works inside enterprise standards, not around them:

This is the governance you already have, applied while you build instead of after.

For us at Polestar Analytics, this is not just what we preach but what we follow. We have forward deployed marketers in industry teams, for example, who get visibility into what the need of the hour is, right where the need is. And many more.

Simply put, the FDE title might be new, but the theory is as old as computers themselves. What’s changed is that the engineer now sits with the business, builds with the business and owns the outcome with the business.

If you’ve followed tech news this summer, you’ve almost certainly come across the term Forward Deployed Engineer or, in short, FDE. On June 30, AWS announced a massive $1 billion investment in a new unit built around this one role. OpenAI had already put more than $4 billion behind its own Deployment Company in May. There’s no end to the news on FDE. All of this for just one role.

So, who are they? A forward deployed engineer is an engineer embedded directly in a customer’s environment to design, build and ship AI or custom software solutions. Palantir, which made the title popular, describes the difference well. A regular engineer builds “one capability, many customers.” An FDE delivers “one customer, many capabilities.”

Polygon is approaching a critical price level as a proposed crypto hard fork puts the network back trending. POL recently recovered toward $0.10, while Binance and Polymarket are seeking to recover millions in stolen tokens through a controversial governance proposal.

The plan could strengthen confidence in Polygon’s ability to protect users, but it also raises questions about decentralization. Can the recovery effort help POL extend its rebound or trigger another round of selling?

Polygon Labs Member Proposes Hard Fork to Recover Approximately 70.49 Million POL Stolen from Polymarket and BinanceA member of the Polygon Labs Validator Support Team has published a Polygon Improvement Proposal (PIP) suggesting a hard fork on the Polygon PoS mainnet to… pic.twitter.com/n8hoCCsYms

The proposed hard fork would zero the balances of four addresses linked to the Polymarket incident and one tied to Binance. Polymarket accounts for 23.86 million POL, while Binance’s address holds 46.63 million POL. The proposal would credit the equivalent balances to recovery wallets verified by the affected platforms.

Polygon block producers have already restricted transfers from the identified addresses. However, the current blacklist prevents movement without returning the assets to their owners.

The proposal would make the recovery permanent through a coordinated network upgrade. It would not create new POL or alter the token’s total supply. Governance discussion is scheduled for today. Approval would still require client development, testing on Polygon’s Amoy testnet, and coordination with validators.

The proposal describes the intervention as an exceptional measure tied to publicly acknowledged thefts and traceable funds. It warns that the action should not become a routine mechanism for reversing transactions.

#5522. Cava hit 500 restaurants ahead of schedule. Its CFO explains how it plans double in size by 2032

Good morning. Cava has reached 500 restaurants ahead of schedule, putting it halfway toward its goal of at least 1,000 locations by 2032. But for CFO Tricia Tolivar, the bigger challenge is ensuring the Mediterranean fast-casual chain can sustain its performance as it doubles in size.

The early results are encouraging. Cava’s newest restaurants are operating at roughly 100% productivity, Tolivar told me, suggesting the company has room to expand into new markets without sacrificing sales performance.

“Even more encouraging is the strength of those new restaurant openings,” she said.

Still, Cava’s rapid expansion comes as consumers face mounting financial pressure. The company reported Wednesday that third-quarter Cava segment revenue rose 22.1% year over year to $353.7 million, while same-restaurant sales increased 3.1%, with guest traffic slightly positive. Consolidated revenue totaled $356.4 million, short of analysts’ estimate of about $358.4 million.

Tolivar attributed about 150 basis points of the same-restaurant sales impact to consumer concerns about fresh produce following a Cyclospora outbreak, even though Cava wasn’t among the chains linked to it. Excluding that impact, same-restaurant sales would have grown roughly 4.6%. CAVA nevertheless raised its full-year same-restaurant sales guidance to 6% to 7%, up from 4.5% to 6.5%.

Cava has been one of the restaurant industry’s strongest performers in recent years, particularly in growth and sales momentum. The challenge now is balancing expansion with operational discipline, particularly as Cava enters new markets and consumers become more cautious about spending.

Tolivar said Cava has kept price increases below inflation over the past six years, while investing in technology and employee development to support growth.

That includes a new operator portal that allows general managers to manage digital orders and update out-of-stock items in real time. The company’s in-house Cava Command Center also consolidates restaurant performance data, replacing separate systems and spreadsheets.

For a chain that now operates in 31 states and Washington, D.C., those investments could become increasingly important. Managing 1,000 restaurants will require more than opening new locations; it will mean maintaining consistent execution, controlling costs and protecting the customer experience across a much larger operation.

Cava reached its 500-restaurant milestone through long-term planning, performance tracking, and adapting as circumstances changed, Tolivar said.

“When curveballs come your way, how do you then pivot and adjust so that you can continue to meet, if not exceed, expectations?” she said. She added that Cava is investing in the business “not for the next 12 weeks, but for the next 12 years and beyond.”

Have a good weekend. Sheryl EstradaSheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

As AI changes how work gets done, managing the people side of that change is becoming a financial priority. Seventy percent of leaders say their most recent transformation initiative fell short of its intended business value, according to a Deloitte report.

Still, the median return on change management investment was 4:1, meaning every $1 invested was associated with $4 in realized business value. Yet 60% of respondents say their company treats change management as a project cost rather than a business capability. AI is adding to the pressure: 61% say AI transformation is moving faster than their employees can handle.

Among leaders overseeing AI implementation, estimated turnover-related costs average $25.5 million. The findings are based on a survey of 1,000 change management leaders in the U.S., U.K., Australia and Canada, about half of whom hold C-suite roles, including CFOs.

#5520. The government can lower grocery prices. It doesn’t have to run the stores

David L. Ortega is a professor and the Noel W. Stuckman Chair in Food Economics and Policy at Michigan State University.

Almost every plan to lower food prices ends up putting the government in one of two businesses, either running a grocery store, as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is now doing, or telling grocery stores what to charge. A new proposal from the Kitchen Table Project does neither, which is why I’ve spent more time with it than I expected to. Instead of working on what shoppers pay, it works on what the store pays.

The federal government already buys an enormous amount of food. USDA runs competitive auctions to supply school lunch and other nutrition programs, and it has been doing so for decades. The proposal would let any grocer, whether a bodega in the Bronx or a Kroger in Lansing, buy a basket of 20 staples at a similar auction price. The one condition is that the store has to sell them at a markup that’s set in advance and posted where customers can see it.

This is like a Costco membership where Washington is the buying club and the grocer is the member. The government never owns a store, never runs a warehouse, and never writes a check to cover the gap between what food costs and what a politician would like it to cost. The report estimates a family of four would save about $315 a year.

I’m more sympathetic to this than I usually am to grocery proposals, and the reason is purchasing power. Small stores pay more for the same case of eggs because they buy fewer cases. Price surveys consistently show the big discounters undercutting most supermarkets, and the Atlanta Fed has found that food inflation ran hottest in lower-income metro areas, where shoppers have fewer stores to choose from. If a corner store could buy at something close to Walmart’s price, that’s a form of relief neither a price cap nor Mamdani’s city-run supermarkets can offer. New York is paying for a 30 percent discount at five stores, while this proposal would reach every store that signs up. And since the markup is public, shoppers would have a number to hold their regular supermarket against. This also gives other supermarkets a reason to watch their prices.

But for six of the 20 items, which include eggs, milk and ground beef, the report shows no savings at all. I don’t think that’s a flaw in the design so much as a reminder of where food prices come from. Ground beef is close to $7 a pound because the U.S. cattle herd is the smallest it has been in 75 years. No auction or purchasing plan, however large, produces more cows. I’d also bet against the federal government out-negotiating Walmart and Costco, which have spent decades on procurement and are very good at it. If Washington simply matched what the big chains pay, that would still be a meaningful help to independents, and it’s worth doing. It’s just a smaller promise than the headline number suggests.

Which brings everything back to the markup. The report doesn’t say who sets it. Rent and wages in the Bronx are not rent and wages in Lansing, and a single national margin could end up either squeezing out the stores the program is meant to help or leaving so little room that the discount barely shows up on the shelf. The chains that already get good terms may look at the paperwork and decide it isn’t worth it.

There’s a second-order problem too. A grocer selling 20 items at a capped margin still has to make payroll, and the obvious way to do that is to increase prices on the other several thousand items in the store. A family could save on the program staples, lose it on everything else, and never know the difference.

Even so, this is the first grocery proposal I’ve seen in a while that tries to lower prices through competition rather than by having taxpayers absorb the difference. That alone makes it worth piloting. Name the markup. Say who can join. And then judge it by what a family actually saves on the whole cart, not on a handful of staples.

#5518. Their Kids Loved The Little Gym. Then They Saw a $20 Million Franchise Opportunity.

Griffin Gordon and Kevin Condon were The Little Gym customers before they became franchise investors. Now they own 30 gyms.

Before Griffin Gordon and Kevin Condon owned dozens of The Little Gym locations, they were parents watching their children enjoy gymnastics classes at the franchise. Their kids were tumbling, running and leaving class asking to do it all again.

As a customer, Gordon was impressed that The Little Gym staff members knew the children’s names, greeted their parents and made families feel welcome.

Gordon and Condon had met years earlier at the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business before pursuing different careers. Condon became a co-founder of Hidden River Strategic Capital, a Philadelphia-based private equity firm that invests in small businesses. Gordon split his career between private equity investing and running small and midsize companies, later founding an investment firm focused on franchisees.

Their paths converged around an opportunity involving Richard Moore, a longtime Little Gym operator whose family had spent nearly three decades building the business. Moore wanted to keep growing. His parents were ready to retire. An advisor introduced him to Gordon and Condon, who saw a chance to pair an experienced operator with the capital and support to expand.

In 2023, Gordon and Condon’s firms invested in seven North Carolina locations of The Little Gym, forming the foundation of a business called Somersault. Three years later, the partners say their footprint has grown to more than 30 locations, with another 10-plus in development. Their business generates nearly $20 million in revenue.

They credit that expansion to a combination of familiar ingredients, including an established brand. Here’s why they decided to invest in The Little Gym and open new franchise locations.

The following interview has been lightly edited for clarity and concision.

Why invest so aggressively, growing from seven locations to more than 30?Kevin Condon: Ultimately, we’re backing management teams and organizational leaders. We have a really good team here, which has allowed us to scale at this pace and given us the conviction to continue putting money behind the business.

The other piece is the repeatable process in franchising. You acquire a business or open a location, and you have a playbook. With a good team and good operators, you can repeat that playbook. We’ve taken a strong brand and expanded through acquisitions and new openings.

Griffin Gordon: Kevin’s firm has done a lot of franchisee investing. My firm focuses solely on it. The Little Gym has the things we find attractive: a growing market of parents who want high-quality services for their kids, a strong brand and attractive unit economics when the business is operated well.

What else made this particular opportunity attractive?Gordon: In our view, The Little Gym is the best brand serving its target age range. There are imitators, but we don’t think they match the quality of its curriculum and operating playbook.

We also have a strong franchisor partner in Unleashed Brands. To invest in franchisees, you need a partnership approach and confidence that the franchisor values that relationship, too.

How did those factors turn into an actual investment?Gordon: It was equal parts purposeful and opportunistic. We were interested in franchisee investing because of its repeatability and scalability. We were also focused on child enrichment because we thought it was an attractive market if you did things right.

How much did being customers influence your decision to start locations of your own?Condon: We only have so much time and money to allocate. The Little Gym offered the opportunity to invest in what we consider a category leader in youth enrichment, particularly children’s recreational gymnastics and related activities.

The system has been around for 50 years. This year was its 50th anniversary, which was a major milestone for the franchise.

There’s an established playbook, and both our business and the overall system are growing. When you have a strong brand and the unit economics to open a location, ramp it up and become profitable, you can create returns for investors, jobs for employees and outcomes for families. That makes it easy to understand why we want to continue investing our time and money.

What are the most important elements of that repeatable playbook?Gordon: There are two sides to it: the fundamentals that don’t change, and the opportunity to modernize the business for today’s parents and children. The fundamentals include building and investing in a great team, genuinely caring about the curriculum and developing authentic connections with the communities where you operate.

How do those fundamentals connect with changes to the business?Gordon: You also have to work with the franchisor to make sure the curriculum supports the outcomes everyone wants: Confident, self-assured, well-adjusted children who have an opportunity to become physically active early in life.

That dovetails with Unleashed Brands’ investments in infrastructure. Before our investment, The Little Gym didn’t have much in the way of technology, systems and infrastructure. It operated more like a small-business-owned enterprise.

Since Unleashed Brands’ acquisition, we’ve been able to combine the traditional strengths of the business with improvements in the technology we use to operate it and the systems customers interact with.

There’s also been a more thoughtful approach to customer acquisition and marketing, alongside continued investment in the programming. The offering has to remain competitive with parents’ changing demands and schedules.

Condon: The core curriculum is the secret sauce. It’s been part of what has made The Little Gym special for 50 years. But you can build on that. For example, Unleashed introduced an app this year to help parents engage with their children’s classes and see milestones and pictures.

That’s something that obviously didn’t exist 50 years ago. It connects what The Little Gym has historically done well with what a modern parent wants from a class.

Both of you have children who attended. What were their experiences like?Condon: Smiles from ear to ear. They’d spend 45 to 60 minutes in class, come out sweaty and exhausted, and their first question would be, “Can we do that again?”

There’s a joy in watching children move and take appropriate risks, whether they’re learning a cartwheel or somersault, jumping, running, singing, following directions or engaging with other kids.

Much of what I’m describing is in that 2-to-6-year-old age range, although we serve younger and older children, too. I saw it with my own kids, and we see it across the children coming through our locations. There’s a consistency to that experience. It’s unadulterated childhood joy.

Why franchise instead of starting an independent business?Condon: In small business, the opportunity to be part of something with a name as established as The Little Gym is attractive. We invest in both franchised and non-franchised businesses. One benefit of franchising is that you can be part of something much bigger than you could create on your own.

If we started a competitor, we wouldn’t have 50 years of history or an established brand. Franchising gives us an affiliation with a much larger organization and system.

You pay royalties and operate within certain rules. But in this case, we believe the playbook and brand provide more benefits than going it alone.

Gordon: When done correctly, franchising should be like buying a small business with the benefit of a national platform. Those two things should work together. That’s what we believe we have with The Little Gym.

What should someone do if they’re interested in franchising but don’t know where to start?Gordon: One of the best things about franchising is the availability of information. Not every detail is public, but the information you need to understand the model is there.

In particular, there’s a list of franchisees in the back of the franchise disclosure document. If you’re evaluating a system, start calling owners and learning from them. These are people who have already done what you’re trying to do. I can’t think of a better resource.

Condon: Find something you’re passionate about, particularly if you’ll be the operator. Even if you won’t operate the business yourself, you still need to care about it. In our case, as investors helping build and scale a company, we also need an operator who knows how to execute the playbook successfully.

What lesson have you learned while building the company?Gordon: The lesson we’ve learned and continue to learn is that this business is all about people. People sometimes hear about The Little Gym and think it sounds simple. It’s a simple business to understand, but a challenging business to operate well.

The business depends on our ability to find the best people, train them effectively and give them career opportunities. That might mean moving beyond a teaching role, taking on more responsibility within a gym or eventually overseeing multiple locations.

What milestones are you working toward? Could revenue eventually reach $100 million?Condon: That sounds great.

Gordon: We’ve gone from seven locations to more than 30 in three years. We’ve quadrupled our footprint. Doing that again over the next couple of years would be aggressive, but we’re big believers in the brand and our business, and we want to keep growing.

#5517. Amazon rewrites its software engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 12:26 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 12:36 pm

Last month, a small team inside Amazon Web Services called Velocity Labs went from concept to the public release of a new open-source AI model in less than a week.

The group, whose existence hasn’t been previously reported, was formed in April. Velocity Labs has about 35 people, most of them in Seattle. The idea is to think beyond Amazon’s normal product-oriented approach, building quick prototypes in areas of AI that the company sees as underexplored and increasingly important to customers.

“We have noticed how the open-source community, and some of our competitors, experiment with new ideas, and deliver initial products fast,” the company says in job listings. “With Velocity Labs we are building an organization that can move faster, explore more, and make sure AWS is at the cutting edge of innovation in agentic AI.”

Inside the group, scientists and engineers work together, and they’re encouraged to cross over: engineers engage in research, and scientists do engineering work.

Velocity Labs is an example of the ways Amazon is trying “to create organizations that we think are going to be better suited to working with this new set of tools,” said Marc Brooker, an AWS vice president and distinguished engineer who leads the team.

For the vast majority of Amazon’s developers, he said, AI agents now write almost all the code that would have previously been written by hand.

Redefining the role: The team is part of Amazon’s larger rethinking of software development for the AI era, laid out in revised guidelines that the company’s engineering leaders sent to its developers earlier this year.

A letter that accompanied the guidelines, published last week under the byline of Michael “Terk” Terkowitz, a VP and distinguished engineer in Amazon’s stores business, advises engineers to learn AI now and to stay close to their customers and products.

The letter acknowledges that as Amazon has grown, some engineers and managers have become “less connected to their customers and business.”

Amazon has never published its underlying role guidelines for software engineers, and it declined to provide a copy of the revised version for this article. Brooker, one of the authors of the accompanying letter, said in an interview that the update emphasizes measuring engineers and teams by outcomes rather than inputs.

“We had seen these anti-patterns in the industry of folks really focusing on how many tokens are you spending, how many lines of code are you committing,” Brooker said, explaining that those kinds of measures don’t equate to customer value.

Asked whether AI use is part of performance reviews or promotions, Brooker said, “Not directly in a metrics sense.” It could factor in, he said, to the extent that it makes someone a stronger performer.

The letter doesn’t dismiss usage metrics entirely. Amazon has found that they “correlate well with the outputs that matter” and expects that to continue “for some time,” it says.

But what’s important, the letter says, is to use them “with care and judgement.”

Amazon engineers have described pressure to use AI tools. Three developers told The New York Times last year that managers were pushing them to use AI, raising output goals and becoming less forgiving about deadlines, with some coders saying their jobs had begun to resemble warehouse work. Amazon has set a goal for more than 80% of its developers to use AI each week, the Financial Times reported.

In May, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard called KiroRank — which ranked employees by how much they used Kiro, the company’s AI coding tool — after finding that some were using the tool excessively just to climb the rankings, the FT reported.

Asked whether that episode was part of the impetus for the revised guidelines, Brooker said he didn’t recall the leaderboard or the details surrounding it.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions.”

Letter accompanying the revised SDE role guidelines

How the work has changed: Two years ago, most Amazon developers were still writing their code by hand, Brooker said. Today, “for the vast majority of our developer population, almost all of their implementation code is agent generated rather than human written,” he said.

“That is a massive change in the way of working for software engineers,” he said.

Brooker said he used to spend much of his time in a traditional code editor or the command line, and now spends a lot more of it working with agent tools such as Kiro, Kiro Crew and Anthropic’s Claude Code, calling it “a complete change of tools.”

For the company, the transition hasn’t been seamless. In March, Amazon acknowledged that an engineer who followed inaccurate advice from an AI agent contributed to one of several outages on its retail site, though the company disputed a Financial Times report that junior and mid-level engineers would need senior engineers to sign off on AI-assisted changes.

Amazon also pushed back on an earlier FT report that a 13-hour disruption to an AWS service in December happened after engineers let its Kiro AI coding tool make changes, and the tool decided to “delete and recreate the environment.” Amazon blamed user error — a misconfigured role — and said it has since added safeguards, including mandatory peer review for production access.

Still, the letter acknowledges that today’s AI tools won’t help in every situation, and it says that’s OK as long as engineers can explain why.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the letter says. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Inside Velocity Labs: The group is part of the agentic AI division led by Swami Sivasubramanian, which has organized much of its work around small teams of six to eight people, as GeekWire reported in June. Velocity Labs also includes the developers behind Strands, AWS’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

The model that Velocity Labs released last month, Strands Decider 2B, is designed to make quick, narrow decisions inside AI agents, such as which tool to use or where to route a request. It’s based on Qwen, an open model from Alibaba, and was released Oct. 1 along with the recipe used to train it.

Brooker built the original version on his own GPU at home after the startup TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, a similar decision model, on Sept. 15, he wrote on his blog. “Every line of code was written by an agent,” he wrote, though he tried to make sure “the core ideas and insights were mine, or at least I understood them.”

Brooker described the team’s turnaround as less than a week from concept to public release. OpenAI announced a similar hosted service, its Decisions API, the same week, TechCrunch reported.

Brooker credited the team’s speed to its small size and a high level of trust: each person takes ownership of a piece of a project and asks for help when needed. He expects Amazon to create more teams like it, though not across the whole company.

Impact on jobs: Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since late 2025. CEO Andy Jassy has said he expects AI to shrink the company’s corporate workforce over time.

At the same time, AWS CEO Matt Garman said in April that Amazon is “hiring just as many software developers as we ever had,” Business Insider reported. An Amazon spokesperson told the publication that more than 11,000 interns and early-career software engineers would join the company globally this year.

Asked whether AI will mean fewer engineers at Amazon, Brooker said, “I don’t think it changes the number of engineers.” The company wants engineers who take ownership, are curious and can learn quickly outside their areas of expertise, he said.

AI isn’t the right answer for every problem, Brooker said.

If the right tool is “an AI agent powered by a cutting-edge model, fantastic,” he said. However, he added, if it’s “three lines of Python code, that’s great too.”

#5516. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5515. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5514. Everyone Has AI Now. Your Next Competitive Advantage Is the People You’re Ignoring.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is no longer a differentiator in the workplace. Human computing power (in collaboration with AI) is the new focus.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Everyone is in an unavoidable race to develop, deploy and integrate AI solutions that give their business operations an edge. The difficulty, at this point, is that AI is available to everyone. Yes, one person can use it more efficiently than the next, but as a new generation of AI-native workers enters the workforce, the “we use AI better than the next guy” advantage is shrinking.

Thoughtful leaders should be using AI, but while it can automate tasks, it can’t eliminate distractions, improve conversations or change how people experience the spaces where they work. As this new digital transformation charges ahead, many teams are overlooking the physical environments that quietly shape their human performance each day.

When you step back, it’s easy to see that AI adoption is no longer the game-changing factor it once was. Instead, workplace design is the next competitive differentiator that will help human teams amplify their AI outputs the best.

AI has many functions and the list of its capabilities is growing all the time. It’s hyper-efficient. It’s good at synthesizing data. It’s cost-effective and can scale without much trouble.

But it is still software. It’s controlled by algorithms. It’s trapped in a machine (even the “Cloud” has to run off physical data centers). That means it can’t address many of the physical human needs in the workplace like when it comes to how people operate and collaborate.

As AI advances, the computing power of the human brain is the part of the equation that is starting to become a deciding factor. The speed (or lack thereof) at which humans can use AI can quickly become a limiting factor in its impact.

The struggle is that it isn’t digital computing power but physical environments that have the most influence on cognitive performance. For instance, Harvard School of Public Health found that simple things like better indoor air quality can affect cognition and, by extension, productivity.

Something like office air pollution isn’t a factor that Claude can compute, or Gemini can jerry-rig. It requires physical solutions and a human mind to design, create and deploy.

It’s important to shift mindsets here when it comes to office environments. Buying that air purifier, for example, isn’t just a health benefit carried over from the past few years of safe distancing. It’s a chance to improve the thinking and performance of your team.

That’s your first step. Stop seeing basic office environmental things like better lighting or cleaner air and water as fundamental requirements. Look at them as investments that give you an edge.

It’s essential that leaders realize how the advantages are shifting. Three years ago, using AI when a competitor wasn’t doing so was a clear advantage. Now, everyone has AI, but those with the best human work environments have the best chance at creating a synergistic advantage through the combination of their machine and human elements.

Investing in overlooked competitive advantages like clean air, low sound, better lighting and other workplace design elements can help:

All of these are more than employee benefits. They are competitive advantages that increase performance through environments that are not just AI-powered but are also human-aligned.

The key is finding ways to incorporate human advantages in a workspace that are as low-lift as possible. Take sound as an example. How loud or “noisy” a space is will impact people’s concentration. What makes a space “noisy” is something called reverberation time, explains RPG Acoustical System, which is the amount of time it takes for sound waves to get below certain decibels. The longer it takes, the noisier a room sounds.

Leaders can take this into consideration when designing or arranging workspaces. They can make sound waves decrease more quickly through the use of sound-absorbing elements, such as rugs or fabrics hung on the wall, wood furniture pieces and drop ceilings.

AI in the workplace is about more than productivity. Artificial intelligence is hyper-productive in a way that humans are just starting to comprehend. It can produce at such a prodigious level that, in most areas of work, the need to have more output won’t be the problem moving forward.

Instead, employers should be designing workplaces that support better work. As machines crank up the output in nearly every work environment, the offices with the highest-performing human workers will have the best chance of producing the highest-quality work. This makes optimizing human cognition and collaboration a priority.

It is an advantage that few leaders are thinking about as everyone races to invest more in the latest AI solutions. Don’t stop investing in AI, but start thinking about your human workers again, too. Investing in overlooked areas like workplace design can be the quiet way to give yourself an advantage in the AI/human world that is unfolding.

Everyone is in an unavoidable race to develop, deploy and integrate AI solutions that give their business operations an edge. The difficulty, at this point, is that AI is available to everyone. Yes, one person can use it more efficiently than the next, but as a new generation of AI-native workers enters the workforce, the “we use AI better than the next guy” advantage is shrinking.

Thoughtful leaders should be using AI, but while it can automate tasks, it can’t eliminate distractions, improve conversations or change how people experience the spaces where they work. As this new digital transformation charges ahead, many teams are overlooking the physical environments that quietly shape their human performance each day.

When you step back, it’s easy to see that AI adoption is no longer the game-changing factor it once was. Instead, workplace design is the next competitive differentiator that will help human teams amplify their AI outputs the best.
