#5445. A YC startup is putting $1M behind 5 unsolved materials science problems for AI

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Discovered Materials, a months-old San Francisco startup using AI models to find new substances for building advanced chips, announced a million-dollar challenge for AI models to solve five critical problems in materials science.

While frontier AI models have solved a remarkable series of outstanding mathematics problems and made progress in the life sciences, they have yet to truly plumb the complex physics in advanced materials.

“It’s more difficult to specify problems clearly in materials science because it’s not like math, where you have a very specific definition and can get to a yes or no,” said Advaith Sridhar, a co-founder of Discovered Materials, which was part of Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch. “We came to this discussion [wondering], what are the grand challenges in this field? How do we know AI is making progress?”

Though materials science doesn’t have an equivalent of the Millennium Prize Problems, Discovered Materials recruited an advisory group of academics at leading global universities to spell out five open problems. The company is offering a pool of prizes, worth $1 million in total, for solutions to the problems.

“Across materials science, there are phenomena we observe but cannot explain,” Felipe Jornada, a Stanford professor who helped develop the challenges, said in a statement. “Explaining these phenomena would improve our understanding of physics, and the answers would directly shape how we build electronics, store energy, and manufacture the materials of the future.”

Before announcing the challenges, Discovered Materials turned frontier lab models loose on them, giving AI agents internet access and other resources to work autonomously for days. The models spent several days on each problem without making much headway. Still, it’s easy to imagine OpenAI or Anthropic attempting to one-shot them with significantly more compute or a newer model.

“It’s not particularly a concern to us whether we find it, or someone else finds it, or a professor finds it, or the frontier labs find it,” Sridhar said. “The reason we’re putting out these challenges is because we want them to serve as the goalposts. If you go and solve these challenges, we are deepening our understanding of materials and how things around us behave.”

Tracking efforts to solve the problems will show “whether the models are climbing in this domain,” he added.

The challenge also reflects the changing nature of scientific inquiry as AI proves capable of uncovering insights and techniques human researchers didn’t anticipate. With solutions apparently easier to find than ever, the questions become more important.

“This is a new way of thinking about science, where we come up with the verification and the challenges first, and then we let somebody come up with the ideas that explain the problem,” Sridhar said. “Knowing what are the right questions to ask is not trivial and very difficult in this domain, so this is where the professors have really helped us shape what are the right questions we should be asking.”

Discovered Materials’ main focus is developing new materials for use in semiconductors; the startup partners with chip giants on research projects while also funding its own scientific efforts. When the company announced its seed round in August, Sridhar told TechCrunch that he hoped the company would generate a useful material within a year.

“Those timelines have accelerated a little bit,” he says today. “I’m more confident now that we will be able to find these industrially useful materials in a timeline shorter than a year.”

Bitcoin (BTC) traded near $76,900 on Tuesday, November 3, as Americans voted in midterms that Polymarket traders see Democrats sweeping, 76.5% for the Senate and 94.5% for the House, a result that could push crypto’s market structure law to 2027 or later.

The industry spent big to stop that. Crypto-linked groups have put more than $200 million into this cycle. Yet the bill they most wanted, the CLARITY Act, is still stuck in the Senate, seven weeks after a 49-50 vote left it 11 votes short.

Now the clock is the problem. Any bill that hasn’t passed when this Congress ends on January 3 dies with it, and the next Congress would have to start from scratch.

BTC USD price itself is down 1.3% in 24 hours and 9.8% over the past month, and it is sitting right on its 200-day average. Spot ETFs lost $398.6 million on Monday, and the Fear & Greed Index reads 26.

So how long could a Democratic Congress hold up crypto laws, and does the market care?

One law is done, the other is stalled. The GENIUS Act, the stablecoin law, was signed in July 2025, and Treasury says its rules are on track. The CLARITY Act never made it through the Senate. It would decide when a token falls under the SEC or the CFTC.

The House passed it 294-134 on July 17, 2025. The Senate Banking Committee advanced its version 15-9 in May. Then, on September 15, a vote to open debate failed 49-50 when it needed 60.

Almost certainly for this bill. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for the Senate, and prediction market traders gave them a 74% chance on Monday, the highest since the market opened.

The only route left for the current text is the lame duck session between the election and January. NYDIG’s Greg Cipolaro said in May that it works only if Republicans keep the Senate and Majority Leader John Thune puts it ahead of government funding deadlines. If Democrats win, he said, the bill is unlikely to move when the new Congress starts.

The White House isn’t counting on it either. “There’s no holding them back in hopes of a lame duck passage of the bill,” crypto adviser Patrick Witt said in September, pointing the SEC and CFTC to write rules on their own.

A Democratic Senate would also hand the gavels to people who voted against this bill. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Banking Committee, opposed it in May and would be in line to chair it. Expect a new draft with:

Then there is the White House. President Trump has already said that if Democrats win the House, “I guess I’ll become Mr Veto.” A bill both sides can pass, and he will sign, means starting over in 2027.

"I guess I'll become Mr. Veto."President Trump lays out his strategy for dealing with a potential Democratic-controlled Congress in an exclusive interview with Miranda Devine.Trump says he would veto legislation before eventually negotiating compromises, while expressing hope… pic.twitter.com/n63QdC5MV0

Former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, now on OKX’s board, called it “a hostile Congress” for the industry. Still, not everything stops: regulators’ rules don’t need a vote, though without a law behind them, they are easier to challenge in court and to reverse under the next president.

Barely. BTC trades at $76,903, just above the 200-day EMA at $76,504, and 39% below its $126,080 record from October 2025.

A Democratic sweep is mostly priced in. The surprise would be a Republican Senate, which would reopen the lame duck window for the CLARITY Act.

#5442. Why Coinbase Bitcoin Discount Just Hit a Yearly High

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Classic crypto market metrics have suddenly stopped reflecting reality. Bitcoin’s discount on the U.S. exchange Coinbase relative to the international Binance has hit a yearly high, with the Coinbase Premium Index collapsing to around −0.06%.

In normal times, such a chart gives traders a cold sweat: the index going deep into the red zone means that large funds in the U.S. have started massively dumping crypto.

However, the current collapse of the indicator turned out to be a technical illusion. It was provoked by the emergency freeze of operations on Binance immediately after a large-scale hack of the exchange, which completely blocked classic cross-exchange arbitrage.

The anomalous price gap coincided with the largest incident in the industry’s history: on October 29–30, hackers attacked Binance’s hot wallets, withdrawing about $6.3 billion. The exchange promptly froze half of the stolen funds on the blockchain, and the head of the platform promised to fully cover the remaining client losses from the SAFU reserve fund.

Nevertheless, amid the panic, the price of Bitcoin dropped to $77,000–$78,000.

To localize the problem, Binance completely shut the gateways — it temporarily banned any deposits and withdrawals of funds. This decision instantly paralyzed cross-exchange arbitrage. Large players physically could not buy the temporarily cheaper Bitcoin on Coinbase and transfer it to Binance to even out the price.

Liquidity was locked inside the platforms, which caused the discount to artificially swell to its widest level in a year.

As noted by Galaxy Research’s head of research Alex Thorn, due to the blocking of transactions, the discount on Coinbase temporarily stopped being a signal of weak demand in the U.S.

On November 1, Binance announced a phased reopening of withdrawals, starting with BTC and ETH. Now the market is waiting to see how quickly arbitrageurs eliminate the gap. If the gap closes in the coming days, it means the anomaly was purely technical.

If the negative spread becomes entrenched, it will be an alarming signal of a real cooling of American capital.

#5441. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5440. Aina’s smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.

The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.

The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.

Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the new ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.

Now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01, Sandbar Stream, Oasis, and Natura, which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.

For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.

I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format, with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.

It’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.

“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.

Companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller. The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.

Aina’s ring goes on preorder starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company plans to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.

#5439. Nvidia, Nike and 48 Other Companies Oppose OKX Stock Tokenization Plan

A total of 50 companies, including Nvidia (NVDA) and Nike (NKE), have officially raised objections to the trading of tokenized shares on a new platform backed by crypto exchange OKX and the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).

As per the most recent public notice by the joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), OKXICE, the total number of companies objecting to the initiative has reached 50 as of Oct. 30.

The total increased from 38 companies on Oct. 28, with 12 additional companies raising objections in just two days.

The new names that recently raised objections include Nvidia, Nike, Costco (COST), Micron Technology (MU) and Reddit (RDDT).

Other companies that have recently raised objections include cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike (CRWD), Corning (GLW), Bloom Energy (BE), IREN (IREN), USA Rare Earth (USAR), Palo Alto Networks (PANW) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE).

Big names in the financial world, including JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Goldman Sachs (GS) and Wells Fargo (WFC), have also raised objections.

Some other prominent names include Walmart (WMT), Coca-Cola (KO), McDonald's (MCD), Eli Lilly (LLY), Adobe (ADBE) and Dell Technologies (DELL).

OKXICE is a joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE). Each of them owns a 50% stake in the joint venture.

The goal is to enable tokenized versions of traditional US stocks to be traded on the blockchain.

Instead of buying these shares on a traditional brokerage platform, eligible investors can trade blockchain tokens that represent ownership interests in the underlying securities.

The platform will be open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, as per the company's public notice.

The planned platform will be based on a temporary regulatory exemption issued by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Sept. 17.

However, the regulator gave companies the option to object to any unauthorized third-party tokenization of their shares.

If a company submits an objection within the specified timeframe, then its third-party tokenized shares cannot be offered by the platform under the exemption.

#5438. XRP Price Prediction: Wall Street’s $28 Target Hinges on Supply Shock

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is trading near $1.30 as institutional demand and tightening supply return to the spotlight. Standard Chartered still sees XRP price reaching $28 despite cutting its near-term prediction.

The bank’s target would require XRP to climb more than 2,000% from current levels. That makes institutional adoption and sustained buying pressure central to the bullish case.

U.S. spot XRP ETFs have accumulated 1.2 billion XRP since launching. Meanwhile, Ripple’s escrow system continues releasing tokens, creating a potential clash between institutional demand and available supply.

Standard Chartered’s Geoffrey Kendrick lowered his 2026 XRP price target to $2.80 earlier this year. However, the bank maintained its long-term forecast of $28 by 2030. Its revised roadmap projects XRP reaching $7 in 2027, $12.60 in 2028, and $19.60 in 2029. The final $28 target would represent an extraordinary recovery from current prices.

At approximately $1.30, XRP would need to gain around 2,050% to reach $28. Its market capitalization would approach $1.8 trillion using today’s circulating supply.

This valuation would place XRP among the world’s largest financial assets. ETF demand alone cannot justify such a move without substantial growth in adoption and liquidity.

Kendrick’s bullish thesis relies on institutional participation, regulatory clarity, and greater use of blockchain payment infrastructure. Spot ETFs provide one potential route for traditional investors to gain exposure.

The question now is whether those products can absorb enough XRP to influence market supply.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

U.S. spot XRP ETFs held 1.2 billion XRP by November 4. That accounts for 1.2% of the token’s fixed 100 billion maximum supply.

The funds have accumulated substantial holdings since their launch. However, recent flows show that institutional demand has not been consistently positive.

ETF data recorded outflows during several recent sessions, while October’s strongest buying days were followed by withdrawals. This could create a supply squeeze with renewed and sustained inflows.

If ETF demand accelerates, issuers must acquire XRP to support their products. Those purchases could reduce the amount of XRP readily available for trading, particularly if existing holders refuse to sell.

That dynamic could amplify price movements during periods of rising demand. A genuine supply shock would require persistent buying to overwhelm available sellers across exchanges and other markets.

Ripple’s escrow system adds another layer to the XRP price prediction. The company releases up to one billion XRP from escrow each month, with unused tokens often returned to new escrow contracts. Ripple is reportedly holding 31.7 billion XRP in escrow. Its total XRP holdings stood at 36.8 billion.

The negative impact of the 31 October release by Ripple of 300 million XRP from escrow🤣. $1.23 to $1.31. It’s as if XRP moves with the market or something. pic.twitter.com/OX3md8GTP1

But could XRP touch $28? The bullish scenario would require ETF purchases and institutional accumulation to outpace selling pressure. Greater use of XRP in payments and tokenized financial markets could provide additional demand.

XRP price remains far below Standard Chartered’s long-term prediction, for now. The token’s ability to hold recent support and attract renewed ETF inflows will help determine the supply-squeeze thesis and whether it can gain traction.

A sustained institutional buying cycle could strengthen the case for a much larger rally. Reaching $28, however, would require years of adoption growth beyond the ETF market alone.

#5437. Zipline hits $21.5B valuation as Walmart expands bet on drone delivery

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.

Zipline and Walmart reached a new multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. The two companies have had a drone delivery agreement since 2021, but this deal is a significant jump from the 21 active drone delivery sites they have together today.

On the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest, and Salesforce Ventures. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.

The company, which has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software, said it plans to use the funds to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire more workers to build out a nationwide drone delivery network.

Founded in 2014, Zipline got its start in Africa, where it used its autonomous drones to deliver blood in Rwanda, and later expanded to Ghana and Nigeria. The California-based company began its first operations in the U.S. in 2020, ferrying medical equipment and supplies to Novant Health in North Carolina. The following year, it struck a deal with Walmart.

But it was in 2022 that Zipline’s business really started to take off in the United States. Zipline received its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration that year, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to complete long-range commercial drone deliveries. It has locked in a number of partnerships since then, including with Uber earlier this year.

Zipline now uses its drones to deliver food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several cities in the United States, and Japan. Zipline’s home delivery service uses Zipline’s Platform 2 drones, which are designed to carry up to eight pounds and travel to customers within a 10-mile radius. Its larger Platform 1 drones are used for long-range deliveries for enterprise, business, and government that can cover 120 miles round trip.

The company said Thursday that its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October of this year. This latest funding aims to push that metric even higher.

Something potentially enormous could be approaching for Tesla (TSLA) by January 1, 2027. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that TSLA stock could be a standout performer through Q4 and into 2027, based on a hypothetical landmark catalyst that isn’t impossible.

The concept focuses on Tesla obtaining widespread regulatory approval for unsupervised full self-driving robotaxi operations in several major markets, while also scaling up the production and deployment of Optimus humanoid robots beyond current expectations.

In this scenario, Tesla would quickly shift from primarily an electric vehicle manufacturer to a high-margin platform company centered on autonomy and robotics. This transformation could open up multi-trillion-dollar markets and significantly increase the company’s stock valuation.

On the higher timeframes, TSLA has been consolidating in the $390–$415 region after a recovery from lower levels earlier in the year. Price continues to hold above key intermediate supports while facing resistance around the $420–$450 zone.

In a standard bull market for growth and technology stocks, a sustained breakout above $480–$520 would confirm intermediate strength and open the path to higher-cycle targets.

Under the extreme robotaxi approval and Optimus scaling scenario outlined above, clearing significant resistance levels would likely trigger powerful measured-move extensions and multi-cycle projections from the longer-term base.

Momentum indicators currently sit in neutral-to-constructive territory with substantial room to run into the strong overbought readings typical of high-beta technology rallies.

Key nearer-term supports sit near $380–$390 and $350–$360; holding those levels would keep the broader recovery structure intact.

Tesla may open Optimus reservations in December.Investor Modar Alaoui says Tesla told him so.They'd launch with his Humanoids Summit, Dec 1–2.Optimus V3 is set to be demoed there.Musk expects deliveries to other companies around end of 2027. pic.twitter.com/b2H2qEcl0w

In recent weeks, Tesla has delivered several updates that support longer-term optimism around autonomy and robotics. In its Q3 2026 results, the company beat adjusted EPS estimates and generated positive free cash flow, even as it ramped spending on AI and future products.

More importantly, Tesla confirmed that production of Optimus humanoid robots has begun on high-volume lines in Fremont, marking a shift from prototypes to early manufacturing.

On the autonomy side, the Cybercab robotaxi service continues to expand, with the Austin fleet growing rapidly, plans to launch in Dallas, and an ambition to deliver the first Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026.

Unsupervised robotaxi miles have increased sharply, while Full Self-Driving subscriptions remain on a strong upward trajectory. Tesla has also entered volume production of the Semi.

While near-term profits remain under pressure from heavy investment, these operational milestones reinforce the narrative of Tesla evolving beyond vehicles into high-margin autonomy and robotics platforms.

Under this highly speculative scenario, and assuming supportive market conditions return, Tesla (TSLA) could reach between $1,800 and $3,000, with a stretch target toward $4,500+ by January 1, 2027.

This remains pure speculation and entertainment, not a realistic base-case outlook. The catalyst would require extraordinary regulatory progress and execution on robotaxi and Optimus at a scale that is currently highly unlikely.

Chainlink (LINK): Trading near $11.61, LINK is testing support around $11.00 and looks neutral to bearish in the short term.

Near Protocol (NEAR): Near $4.40, NEAR has a healthy longer-term chart but must hold $4.00–$4.20 to avoid a deeper correction.

Binance Coin (BNB): At about $714, BNB is defending the $690–$700 support zone with a neutral-to-bearish short-term outlook.

Bitcoin (BTC): Near $77,871, BTC is testing $76,000 support, and the short-term outlook is cautiously bearish.

Chainlink is trading at about $11.61, well off its late-September peak near $15.75. On the daily chart, what was a strong bullish run has turned into a corrective consolidation, and right now the price is testing support.

LINK's bullish reversal came in August. It broke above its major moving averages and ran from roughly $8.00 to $15.75. The decline that followed has carved out lower highs and lower lows, and short-term momentum has deteriorated along the way.

The price is now under the shorter-term moving averages, which are bunched around $12.00–$12.60, so sellers still control the near-term trend. Still, LINK is holding above its 200-day moving average near $11.00, and as long as it does, the wider recovery stays intact.

The first support is $11.40–$11.50. Below that sits $11.00, a psychological level. If that gives way for good, the $10.40–$10.60 region comes into view; buyers showed up there recently.

Resistance starts near $12.00–$12.20, and the $12.50–$12.70 supply zone above it is the stronger barrier. Win those back, and a recovery toward $13.30 starts to look more likely.

Daily RSI is around 40–45, on the weak side of neutral. Buying momentum is subdued, but LINK isn't deeply oversold.

There was a sharp wick down toward $10.30 recently, and the price climbed back above $11.50 afterward. That could mean demand is soaking up the selling. One rejection candle doesn't confirm a reversal, though.

Short term, LINK looks neutral to bearish. Its next real move will probably be decided by the $11.00 support and the $12.20–$12.70 resistance zone.

NEAR Protocol trades near $4.40. It had a big rally off its August range of $1.60–$1.80, and even after the latest pullback the bigger structure still looks healthy. Short-term momentum is fading, though, so it may need to consolidate for a while before the next sustained leg up.

The breakout came in September. NEAR tore through several resistance levels and topped out around $6.00 in early October, on much heavier volume than usual, a sign that a lot of the market was taking part.

Since that peak it's been correcting: lower highs, and one test after another of the $4.20–$4.40 support region.

Right now NEAR is trading under its short-term moving averages, with resistance around $4.50–$4.80. The intermediate and long-term averages are still rising and sit well below the price, so the broader bullish structure doesn't look broken yet.

First support is $4.20–$4.30, the area that kept getting tested during the recent consolidation.

Under that, $4.00 is both a psychological and a technical support level. A decisive break there could expose $3.60–$3.70, roughly where the rising longer-period moving average sits.

On the upside, the first resistance is around $4.55–$4.70, then $4.90–$5.00. Break above $5.00 and hold, and the way could open toward $5.40, eventually $5.80–$6.00.

#5433. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5432. 40 Million XRP Moved From Binance Hacker Wallet

Blockchain tracking service Whale Alert has reported that a wallet linked to the massive $6.3 billion Binance hack has just sent 40 million XRP (~$50.5 million) to a mystery address.

On Nov. 2, Whale Alert shared information about the huge XRP transfer, noting that the transaction initiator is an address tagged "Binance Hack 2026."

The huge transfer took place at 03:56 UTC, Whale Alert data shows. The transaction involved 40 million XRP (~$50.46 million).

Interestingly, just 50 seconds before that, Whale Alert reported another transfer of 40 million XRP.

Another 40 million XRP (~$50.44 million) was also sent from the wallet tagged as "Binance Hack 2026" to a mystery address.

In total, these two transfers involved 80 million XRP (~$100.9 million).

Both transfers originated from the same wallet but were sent to separate mystery addresses.

It is still unclear why these transfers were made. There is no sign that these funds have been sent to a crypto exchange or sold yet.

The transactions took place just days after Binance faced one of the biggest cryptocurrency hacks ever.

The massive XRP transfers came shortly after Binance started to restore cryptocurrency withdrawals following the unprecedented security breach the cryptocurrency exchange faced.

On Nov. 1, Binance annonced that the exchange would restore withdrawals in phases for 15 blockchain networks, including XRP Ledger, Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Solana.

It also mentioned that withdrawals would be gradually restored for other networks, such as Tron, Dogecoin, Zcash, Avalanche, Sui, Polygon and Arbitrum.

The first stage of withdrawal resumption was set to take place between 06:00 and 09:00 UTC on Nov. 1.

After Binance faced a security breach on Oct. 29, which led to the loss of around $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from its hot wallets, it temporarily paused withdrawals.

The exchange noted that withdrawals would be restored gradually after the security and infrastructure checks had been performed.

Binance also said that XRP balances were already fully backed, as were those of other major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and BNB.

Binance claimed that, as of Nov. 1, around 95% of affected assets had been replenished. The remaining 5% consists primarily of less liquid cryptocurrencies.

#5431. Hackers Use Claude, Gemini and Kimi to Identify Valuable Crypto Targets

Cybercriminals are using popular artificial intelligence (AI) models like Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini and Moonshot AI's Kimi AI to evaluate the financial worth of potential victims, including those owning cryptocurrencies.

Cybersecurity researchers at Cisco Talos detailed in a new report how a new type of Windows malware dubbed VOLTA-AUTODOXER, or simply VOLTA, steals sensitive data and uses AI tools to identify potentially lucrative targets among compromised users.

Compared to traditional information-stealing malware, which mainly steals passwords and credentials, VOLTA can also analyze stolen data to build victim profiles and determine what assets hackers can potentially exploit for profit.

Notably, one of VOLTA's most dangerous features is its ability to extract sensitive crypto wallet information, including recovery seed phrases, which can potentially give attackers access to digital assets.

VOLTA also includes features that can crack cryptocurrency wallet vaults, posing a big risk for people who store their crypto wallet credentials on their computers.

But its features are not just limited to stealing crypto.

As explained by Cisco Talos security researcher Ryan Fetterman, VOLTA can also grab saved browser passwords, payment card info, authentication tokens, email credentials and active sessions on popular platforms like Telegram, Discord, Steam and Roblox.

It can also extract info from Outlook accounts and Slack workspaces, as well as other personal and professional information on the infected system.

The malware also takes things further by analyzing victims' email accounts to grab more personal data.

For example, it can scan Gmail accounts for purchase confirmations and receipts from services like Amazon, PayPal, Walmart, DoorDash and Uber Eats.

This way, attackers can get more details about a victim's identity, home address, job and spending habits.

The malware can send stolen data to AI models via the OpenRouter service, which provides access to several AI models.

It first tries to process the collected data using Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6.

If the model fails to process the request, VOLTA is hardcoded to try Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.

As explained by Cisco Talos, VOLTA specifically looks for refusal responses before attempting to use a different AI model.

It feeds the collected data to the AI models and asks them to analyze it, providing a comprehensive evaluation of a victim's financial worth.

It can also help identify valuable assets and then rank them based on how lucrative they may be. It can also score a victim's cybersecurity.

Essentially, it allows hackers to use AI models to find potentially lucrative targets without the need to manually sift through stolen data.

#5429. XRP Final Move: Binance Empties Hacked Wallet of Last $101 Million

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. The compromised hot wallet of the Binance exchange has been completely emptied. Blockchain tracker Whale Alert recorded two identical transactions of 40 million XRP each (around $101 million in total), which went to a new address 50 seconds apart.

This is the platform's corporate address rK21t6nGLy4MNDqhvy3pGwcLFy25qgfzMx. After the October 29 attack, the wallet received an official red "Reported as hacked" label in network explorers.

As a result of this final transfer, the address's balance dropped to 23.7 XRP (around $30) — the exchange fully removed the remaining funds, moving them to new internal wallets.

This transfer effectively closes activity on the vulnerable address and is a planned technical consolidation of the remaining balances. The transfer of assets followed a large-scale cross-chain attack on Binance that began on October 29. Total damage across ten different blockchains is estimated at $6.3 billion, making the incident the largest crypto theft in history.

Hot wallets on the XRP Ledger took the first hit: within five minutes at the start of the attack, a total of 233.46 million XRP (around $296 million) was withdrawn from them.

The specifics of the XRPL network itself oblige the exchange to fully zero out hacked addresses. Unlike most stablecoins (such as USDT or USDC), where issuers can forcibly freeze funds, the XRP Ledger code has no protocol-level blocking function.

Neither Ripple nor independent XRP Ledger developers has no technical ability to stop transactions, so leaving any available balance on a hacked wallet is unsafe. Moving the remaining 80 million XRP to new wallets isolated by the platform eliminates the risk of repeated withdrawals.

For the XRP ecosystem, this incident became an absolute all-time negative record, surpassing the September hack of the Bitget exchange, in which 103 million XRP ($157 million) was lost, multiple times over.

At the same time, no panic has been recorded on the market. Binance has fully restored withdrawal operations for clients. The platform's management officially stated that all net user losses will be compensated 1:1 from corporate reserves and SAFU fund money.

The transfer of the last $101 million in XRP likely puts an end to operations with the hacked address, minimizing further technical risks for the platform.

New account creation on the XRP Ledger jumped 142.4%, according to XRPScan data. It points to renewed interest in the ecosystem, even though XRP is still struggling to get its bullish momentum back.

XRPScan counted 7,734 newly activated accounts on November 1, 2026, up 33% from the day before and far above the network's 30-day average of roughly 3,500 new accounts a day.

Wallet creation is clearly speeding up. What's behind it is still unclear.

There are a few plausible explanations. Interest in tokenized assets, stablecoins, and decentralized finance apps on the XRPL may be pushing people to set up new wallets. Exchange onboarding and automated wallet creation could also be adding to the count.

But more accounts doesn't necessarily mean more users. One person can open several accounts, and automated systems can open many more, so other on-chain indicators are needed to judge real adoption.

XRPScan's history also shows account creation has spiked before, with an all-time high of about 30,600 accounts. The latest jump is well short of that.

The network numbers are growing, but the price paints a different picture.

TradingView data from November 2 shows XRP trading near $1.25, after a long correction from its September and October highs. It is still below several major moving averages, so bearish pressure continues to dominate the technical picture.

Immediate support sits around $1.20–$1.25. If XRP tries to recover, the $1.30-$1.35 region could act as resistance.

Rising account creation alongside falling prices reflects blockchain adoption and market demand, which are not the same thing. Stronger confirmation of growing XRPL adoption would need sustained growth in active addresses, transaction volumes, and general use of the ecosystem.

For now, the 142.4% increase is an encouraging sign of network activity. Whether it turns into real demand for XRP is still an open question.

Crypto stocks edged higher before Tuesday’s open, November 3, even as Nvidia, Costco and Nike joined the companies blocking tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, taking the count to 50, and an AI chip sell-off sent Seoul’s Kospi down 3.6%.

The bounce is small, and it follows a bad month. Coinbase traded at $138.74 at 13:00 UTC, up 0.7% from Monday’s close of $137.83, its lowest finish since February 2024. Robinhood, Strategy and Circle rose between 0.5% and 1.1%, and Galaxy led with 2.8% after losing 8.8% on Monday.

The bigger story for the sector is the pushback against tokenization. Objectors to OKXICE, the 24/7 venue for tokenized US stocks that OKX is building with NYSE owner ICE, went from 16 to 50 in 11 days. Today is the deadline for companies notified on October 4, so the list could still grow, while Coinbase, Robinhood and the other crypto names on it have yet to say no.

Asia offered no lift. After a 1.1% drop in the Nasdaq on Monday, Samsung and SK hynix dragged the Kospi to 5,648.79, Shanghai slipped 0.8%, and Tokyo was shut for a holiday. Only Hong Kong closed higher, and Bitcoin held steady through the session at $77,326.

Investors are DUMPING US tech stocks at a rapid pace:The Nasdaq 100 index has dropped -6.1% over the last 3 trading sessions, its biggest 3-day decline since the April 2025 Liberation Day selloff. $QQQ This also marks the 3rd-largest 3-day decline since the 2022 bear market.… pic.twitter.com/jNvmex3HZj

So why are so many companies saying no to tokenization, and why are markets red from Seoul to New York?

Because they would carry the risk and see little of the benefit. OKXICE, the venue OKX is building with NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange, wants to offer round-the-clock trading of US stocks as tokens, paid for in stablecoins.

Under the SEC’s exemption, a company can keep its shares off such a venue if an outside firm does the tokenizing. It has 30 days from notice to object, and the objections have come fast:

The newest 12 are Nvidia, Costco, Micron, CrowdStrike, Corning, IREN, USA Rare Earth, Bloom Energy, Nike, Palo Alto Networks, Reddit and Hewlett Packard Enterprise. They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, which runs its own blockchain unit and says it still likes the technology.

The fight is over shareholder rights, especially votes. “Right now companies like Goldman and Microsoft see all of the risk and none of the upside,” Injective’s COO Mirza Uddin told CNBC.

OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo isn’t backing down. “We are at the very beginning of the rollout of fundamentally different market structure,” he said at the October 30 press conference.

Discover: JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

Only the crypto names avoided objection to tokenisation, along with several major US stocks. Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, Strategy, BitGo and Securitize remain outside the objection list, as do Apple, Amazon, Tesla, SpaceX and Netflix.

One crypto-born company did say no. IREN, the Bitcoin miner that now earns more from renting computers to AI firms than from mining, objected in the latest batch.

Silence isn’t a yes, though. Venues get up to five business days to publish objections, so companies that answered this week may not show up until next week’s notice, and staying off the list doesn’t guarantee a stock will trade at launch.

The AI trade is cracking again. Big Tech results last week showed Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft will keep spending heavily on data centres and chips, and investors want to see faster returns first.

Monday’s selling on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq fell 1.1%, hit Asia’s chipmakers on Tuesday:

Seoul’s slide is the one to watch. The Kospi closed at a record 9,114.55 on June 22 and is now 38% lower, with 17% of that lost since the end of September.

Oil added to the strain. Brent climbed 1.7% to $106.58 after reports of limited US strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after it fell more than 7% on hopes of new talks.

Hong Kong’s crypto stocks split. Exchange operator OSL rose 0.4%, and Boyaa Interactive, which holds Bitcoin, fell 5.1%.

They have been sold off with tech, then sold again for crypto. Every big name is down at least 12% since the end of September, and the first trading day after the Binance hack was the worst of the run.

Coinbase’s daily chart shows how far the slide has gone. The stock is $34 under its 50-day average and more than $50 under its 200-day, and Monday’s close was the lowest since February 2024.

The XRP Ledger (XRPL) is set for a significant week ahead as its long-awaited cleanup upgrade heads for mainnet activation this week, bringing a wide-ranging collection of fixes and improvements to the blockchain.

The fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment, a collection of fixes for Single Asset Vaults, the Lending Protocol, Automated Market Makers, the permissioned DEX, trust lines, NFTs, MPTs, Escrow, Sponsorship, transaction signing, and permission delegation, is at the center of attention, with validator support putting it on track for a potential November 4 activation, provided the required voting threshold of 80% is sustained.

The earliest activation date is Nov 4, 2026 at 2:46 PM UTC, with just 2 days left according to the xrpscan countdown timer.

Some tokens on the XRP Ledger are supposed to be stored in accounts approved by their issuer; however, developers have found a few ways around that rule.

Issuers of regulated assets, such as stablecoins or tokenized funds, can require approval before anyone holds their tokens, typically to perform identity checks first.

Four proposed code changes would resolve the remaining exceptions. All four are included in a single network upgrade dubbed fixCleanup3_5_0.

These have not been merged into the XRP Ledger's main software yet. Once they are, fixCleanup3_5_0 requires support from more than 80% of the network's trusted validators for two weeks before being activated.

According to Hussein Zangana (Vet), director of community at XRP Ledger Foundation, there is a critical Linux kernel vulnerability on kernels 4.4+, affecting any unpatched Linux server in the world with an open IPv4 TCP port. For XRP Ledger node and validator operators who run RHEL 8/9/10, Debian 12/13, Amazon Linux, and Oracle UEK, a fix has already been shipped; they are simply expected to update and reboot.

For those who run Ubuntu, AlmaLinux, Rocky, CentOS Stream, this might not suffice, as they may need to take further steps until a fix is shipped for their distro. They should re-apply the nft rule after a reboot or a flush ruleset reload.

#5425. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) exchange reserves have dropped back to about 85.84 trillion tokens in early November, a level that may be healthier for the meme coin's supply. The price, meanwhile, is still under heavy selling pressure.

The latest on-chain data puts SHIB exchange reserves at 85.8432 trillion tokens, up only 0.01% over the past 24 hours. The seven-day chart tells a different story: reserves have fallen noticeably, which suggests a lot of SHIB has left trading platforms.

Lower exchange reserves generally mean fewer tokens are on hand to be sold. When investors pull SHIB into private wallets, there is less supply available to sellers on centralized exchanges. That doesn't guarantee a price recovery, but it can make the supply picture more favorable.

The reserves are currently valued at about $397.45 million, down 1.69% on the day. Exchange netflow is still positive at roughly 10.94 billion SHIB, so short-term selling pressure hasn't gone away.

The supply picture is improving, but the chart is still bearish. On the daily SHIB/USDT chart, the token trades near $0.00000463 after breaking below its ascending support trendline. It is also under several important moving averages, which means sellers still control the broader structure.

Immediate resistance sits around $0.00000500–$0.00000530. The $0.00000440–$0.00000450 region is the next potential support zone.

If demand starts to recover, the drop in exchange-held supply could matter more. For now, the 85 trillion mark is a constructive on-chain sign, not a confirmed bullish reversal. A more convincing case would need continued exchange withdrawals, stronger buying, and a move back above the key resistance levels.

Other supporting factors include growing concerns about the stability of fiat currencies, ongoing de-dollarization trends among major economies, high fiscal deficits in key nations, and a clear shift by major central banks towards more aggressive monetary easing.

Historically, these factors have led to increased demand for gold and silver as safe-haven assets.

In this speculative scenario, if favorable global conditions for hard assets continue, gold could potentially reach a price range of $8,000 to $12,000 per troy ounce, with a stretch target exceeding $15,000 by January 1, 2027.
